📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In global maritime logistics, Marine Ports and Terminals play a significant role in the movement of container and cargo, within and beyond. Marine ports and terminals world-wide use a Terminal Operating System (TOS) which acts as the central nervous system managing port operations 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. A modern TOS plans, automates and orchestrates every physical and digital activities, resources and events across Order-to-Invoice processes of a marine terminal.

Recent findings suggest that developed by Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), DynaPORT is a field-proven next-generation Terminal Operating System that provides a single, integrated operating backbone for multimodal and multipurpose terminals. It orchestrates the complete order-to-invoice lifecycle across vessel, rail, truck, and barge operations, while supporting containers, general cargo, dry and liquid bulk, break-bulk, and roll-on/roll-off cargo. By automating end-to-end terminal workflows, DynaPORT delivers real-time operational visibility into operations while optimizing assets and resources to drive improvement of key business performance indicators.

Sources indicate that one of India’s largest commercial port developers and operators has relied on DynaPORT for more than two decades across its cargo terminals, supporting the management of bulk, break-bulk, and liquid cargo. To modernize the platform’s architecture, TCS partnered with the customer to achieve a landmark milestone: migrating DynaPORT to a modern, cloud-based architecture.

Recent findings suggest that the Port Operator & TCS partnered with Google Cloud to execute an ambitious cloud modernization journey. Modeled after the architectural principles of high-velocity Google Cloud enterprise transformations—this case study details the systematic deconstruction of legacy technical debt, the strategic rationale and enterprise differentiators of choosing AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, the target Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and AlloyDB cloud-native architecture, the heterogeneous migration of over 1.2 million lines of code using Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS).

Enterprise logistics platforms that evolve over decades inevitably accumulate architectural debt, particularly through tightly coupled components. DynaPORT Cargo followed this pattern: successive releases and architectural transitions gradually transformed the platform into a classic multi-tier monolith, with its components carrying significant technical debt.

Industry observers note that over years of optimization for sub-millisecond on-premises database round-trips, fundamental business logic had been progressively migrated out of the application tier and embedded directly into the database engine. In the DynaPORT Cargo module alone, the core schema contained:.

262 Packages containing over 1.2 million lines of code.

54 Stored Procedures, 53 Functions, and 63 Database Triggers.

Cross-schema User-Defined Types (UDTs).

Critical business operations—such as multi-tiered marine invoice tariff calculations, dynamic slab rating, berth allocation planning, yard truck assignments, and autonomous error logging—were entirely governed by complex, multi-thousand-line PL/SQL procedures. The database was no longer merely a relational persistence store; it was the primary execution engine of the enterprise.

The application tier was hosted on monolithic WebLogic and WildFly application servers running on static on-premises virtual machines. The application relied on legacy Java Enterprise features, including Enterprise JavaBeans (EJBs), custom Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) dialects, and heavy configuration state. Modules including Revenue Management, Berth Planning, Gate Operations, and Reporting shared common JVM heaps across application servers. A performance spike in batch invoice generation could starve memory from real-time Handheld Terminals (HHT) used by container crane operators on the quayside.

Because business logic was fragmented across Java application binaries and raw database packages, continuous delivery was practically non-existent:.

Manual Deployment Runbooks: Releases required multi-hour maintenance windows involving manual execution of sequential SQL scripts, package recompilations, and server restarts.

High Regression Risk: In the legacy schema with 262 interdependent packages, modifying a single package specification frequently invalidated dozens of dependent functions, views, and synonyms, triggering cascading runtime failures.

Environment Drift: Development, testing, and production environments suffered from configuration divergence, requiring lengthy manual reconciliation before any production cutover.

Industry observers note that licensing fees scaled linearly with physical CPU core counts, penalizing the business whenever hardware was scaled to accommodate peak cargo vessel traffic. Furthermore, high-availability setups required complex shared storage arrays, specialized interconnects, and heavy administrative overhead from dedicated database administrators (DBAs).

When architecting the cloud transformation, the joint architecture teams from the customer, TCS, and Google Cloud evaluated two fundamentally different modernization strategies:.

Strategy A: Database-Agnostic Migration.

Strategy B: Modernization using AlloyDB.

Extract all business logic from the database tier and rewrite it into Java application-tier services (HQL / Spring Data).

Retain optimized procedural logic in the database tier, converting to PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL on AlloyDB.

In a recent development, massive. Complete rewrite of thousands of data access objects, ORM mappings, and transaction boundaries.

In a recent development, moderate. Focused remediation of syntax, metadata, and database dialect differences; application remains stable.

Multiple person-years; prohibitive time-to-market.

Target delivery achievable in agile sprints; low operational disruption.

Network latency amplification due to multiple network hops for complex set operations previously run in-database.

Native in-engine execution with sub-millisecond response times, backed by AlloyDB’s accelerated storage and compute engine.

Rejected due to timeline risks and massive business disruption.

Selected as the winning enterprise target path.

The target cloud architecture was designed according to the Google Cloud Architecture Framework, transforming the monolithic JEE middleware into modern containerized microservices orchestrated on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), coupled with an enterprise AlloyDB for PostgreSQL cluster.

The cornerstone of the migration was converting over 1.2 million lines of deeply intertwined Oracle PL/SQL procedural logic into PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL. The team utilized Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS) with its built-in Conversion Workspaces and Gemini-assisted AI code refactoring to accelerate bulk transformations.

In a recent development, while DMS automatically converted the majority of standard DDL constructs, functions, and queries, the remaining (~15%) involved complex Oracle proprietary idioms that required targeted engineering remediation. Couple of examples of the manual intervention.

Technical Pattern & Remediation.

Modernized AlloyDB PL/pgSQL Equivalent.

Architectural Remediation & Runtime Impact.

TYPE_L := array_append(TYPE_L, rec); or TYPE_L[cardinality(TYPE_L)+1] := rec;.

Replaced unsupported .EXTEND method on nested tables with native PostgreSQL array concatenation and dynamic index expansion.

SELECT ROWNUM FROM PTY_IM WHERE ROWNUM <= N;.

SELECT s.idx FROM generate_series(1, N) AS s(idx);.

Eliminated physical dummy table hacks (PTY_IM) in favor of in-memory, set-returning generator functions with zero disk I/O.

Recent findings suggest that in April 2026, the modernized DynaPORT platform on Google Cloud went live in production at one of the newest ports in India, achieving a seamless, low downtime cutover. By Aug’26, 3 more terminals have gone live on this.

Modernized Google Cloud & AlloyDB Stack.

Variable query latency during batch spikes; table bloat requiring manual DBA reindexing.

Upto 2x transactional throughput, sub-second read query responses, automated ML vacuuming and memory optimization.

Complex SAN failover; multi-minute outages during planned database maintenance.

Sub-second automatic failover, 99.99% availability SLA inclusive of maintenance, zero transaction loss.

Multi-week release cycles; high-risk manual database patching; frequent regression issues.

Containerized rolling updates on GKE and non-blocking transactional DDL deployments in AlloyDB.

Punitive per-core enterprise licenses; high on-prem hardware and maintenance overhead.

About 50% reduction in database TCO; completely open-source compatible with transparent, predictable cloud pricing.

Rigid vertical hardware limits; slow hardware procurement cycles.

Instantaneous horizontal elasticity across GKE container pods and AlloyDB read pools.

The successful cloud migration of DynaPORT yields three fundamental architectural lessons for enterprise IT leaders:.

In a recent development, do Not Throw Away Proven Intellectual Property: Fully rewriting mission-critical procedural logic into application code is often a high-risk anti-pattern. Migrating from Oracle PL/SQL to open PL/pgSQL on an accelerated engine like AlloyDB preserves decades of tested business rules while modernizing the infrastructure platform.

Recent findings suggest that select Database Engines Built for Cloud Realities: Standard open-source relational engines often struggle with extreme enterprise throughput without extensive tuning. AlloyDB’s disaggregated storage architecture, columnar acceleration, and built-in ML intelligence provide the enterprise muscle needed to replace legacy commercial database engines.

Containerize Application Workloads on GKE: Decoupling the application tier into independently scalable container pods on Google Kubernetes Engine provides the elasticity and resilience necessary to absorb rapid operational surges without affecting core database stability.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our most powerful model, configured into a new AI foundation for law.
  • For the latest availability and benchmarks, read the November Astra for Law update⁠.
  • Today, we’re introducing Astra for Law: a upcoming foundation for law firms and legal technology companies to build AI products and workflows around their expertise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our most powerful model, configured into a new AI foundation for law.

For the latest availability and benchmarks, read the November Astra for Law update⁠.

Today, we’re introducing Astra for Law: a upcoming foundation for law firms and legal technology companies to build AI products and workflows around their expertise. It combines GPT‑6 Astra, our latest and most powerful model, with settings, tools, and context tailored for professional legal work.

API customers including Harvey and Legora will be able to build on Astra for Law, bringing this intelligence into their own products and workflows. As our frontier models advance, we’ll bring these legal capabilities to our latest models.

We are also expanding our work on privacy and governance to give law firms specific controls for confidential client work. Firms can also customize Astra for Law using our 26 new ecosystem plugins that connect ChatGPT to the specialist tools firms already use, like Relativity and Clio.

Sources indicate that astra for Law combines GPT‑6 Astra with a powerful legal search index and instructions for legal analysis and writing. Together, they amplify Astra’s capabilities across the legal practice, while giving firms and legal technology companies the freedom to build their own applications and workflows.

Our fresh legal search index is one of the tools Astra for Law can use. Legal research often begins with finding the exact right authority, locating the relevant passages, and understanding how relevant and binding they are to the situation at hand. The index helps Astra for Law do that work, and complements the licensed content and specialist products firms rely on from providers such as Thomson Reuters.

Industry observers note that by using the legal search index, Astra for Law can search U.S. case law, statutes, regulations, court rules, and administrative decisions across a corpus of more than 230 million URLs, with sources added daily. Our work with Free Law Project, the nonprofit behind CourtListener, brings its case-law collection covering more than 99.9% of published U.S. precedential case law⁠(opens in a new window) into this research experience.

To measure how this configuration improves legal research, we tested Astra for Law’s complete setup on 200 U.S. legal research questions from the private validation set of Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a new window). This benchmark measures how well the model can find relevant sources and passages, and how well its research answers meet the evaluation criteria.

Sources indicate that at the highest reasoning effort for both systems, Astra for Law passed the evaluation’s overall correctness check on 54.0% of questions, compared with 38.7% for GPT‑6 Astra using web search alone – a 40% relative improvement. Astra for Law also produces more comprehensive answers.

Industry observers note that on case-law-focused questions, Astra for Law found 24% more reference cases than GPT‑6 Astra using web search alone at the highest reasoning effort. On the audited set of target passages, it retrieved up to 54% more relevant passages from the correct court opinions, when comparing the systems at the same reasoning effort.

The result is a stronger research foundation for advising on a deal, assessing a dispute, or developing a legal strategy, with reliable authorities the lawyer can examine for herself.

Astra for Law and GPT‑6 Astra’s performance on the Vals AI Legal Research Bench validation set, across reasoning effort settings.

Legal research is only the first step. Custom instructions for legal analysis and writing guide Astra for Law in applying that research to the client’s facts, developing arguments or deal terms, and identifying weaknesses and uncertainty. That can mean distinguishing a court’s holding from its other observations, addressing cases that weaken an argument, or explaining how a contract exception shifts risk between the parties.

For example, when prompted to identify good law with similar fact patterns, Astra for Law could both pinpoint relevant precedent and match fact patterns better than other frontier models:.

Astra for Law will be initially offered to selected law firms through Trusted Access in ChatGPT and Codex, and will be coming soon to the API. It will appear in the model picker as “GPT‑6 Astra Law” and in the API as gpt-6-astra-law.

Law firms need to protect client confidences and control how AI is used in their practice. We’ve created a special Trusted Access Program for eligible law firms to give lawyers and people working under their supervision access to Astra for Law for professional legal work. For eligible firms, the offering includes Zero Data Retention (ZDR) on our API, and usage of ChatGPT Enterprise is excluded from human review by default.

We are also working with Latham & Watkins, a leader in AI governance, to design for information permissions, ethical walls, client instructions, and firm oversight.

With frontier intelligence and the right controls, firms can turn their own precedents, methods, and judgment into AI tools and workflows built to their standards.

Working with selected firms, our forward-deployed engineers have been adapting ChatGPT Enterprise with custom interfaces and integrations to proprietary data, creating tools for each firm’s workflows:.

Sullivan & Cromwell built an agreement analyzer that brings the firm’s negotiating playbooks and selected precedents into the review of a new deal. It helps lawyers spot risks that emerge when provisions are read together, then turns those findings into proposed redlines and draft client advice they can challenge and refine.

Sources indicate that ropes & Gray built a deal diligence system around how its lawyers work through a data room and decide what matters to the deal. It helps them trace findings back to the source and pinpoint questions that could affect an acquisition, such as whether key customer contracts require notice or consent.

According to recent reports, cooley built GO Public to bring its capital markets expertise into how companies prepare to go public, from drafting the IPO filing to identifying the risks that deserve management’s attention. When the deal changes, it carries that change across the filing so lawyers can review the implications together.

Firms can build with their own teams and partner products, with permitted sources and review processes defined for the work.

According to recent reports, we’re proud to work with the specialist companies who are advancing legal AI. Today, we’re launching 26 partner-built plugins⁠ that help firms go deeper with the tools and knowledge they already use. These plugins cover the practice and business of law. With iManage, a lawyer can draft a negotiation brief in ChatGPT and save it to the matter file; Intapp can surface activities that may need a time entry for review; DeepJudge can bring prior deals into a comparison. Thomson Reuters is bringing HighQ matter context into ChatGPT and previewing a forthcoming CoCounsel Legal connector.

The launch includes 9 community plugins from lawyers and legal engineers at LegalQuants, LECG, and Skills.law, with 47 custom skills that practitioners can adapt, extend, or draw inspiration from to do their work in ChatGPT. Community plugins give the people closest to the work a way to keep setting the standard for what these skills can do. We’re also making ChatGPT for Word generally available today, so lawyers can proofread, get suggested edits, and flag formatting problems in the tool they already rely on for drafting.

Our approach is open and composable: firms can use specialist products, bring their own tools and knowledge, and adapt community-built skills to their practice. Partners can keep developing their own applications and workflows, while firms choose how those capabilities fit together. Building on OpenAI should mean getting more from the ecosystem, not replacing it.

OpenAI is investing in law for the long term. We’ll keep advancing Astra for Law’s model, settings, tools, and instructions together, guided by rigorous evaluations and feedback from lawyers and legal technology partners. We’ll also keep improving ChatGPT so firms can build around their expertise and connect the tools they use.

Our work with Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz brings the firm’s litigation and corporate expertise together with our frontier research and engineering to explore how AI can support the work involved in providing sophisticated legal judgment.

The most ambitious applications will come from the people who practice law and the companies building alongside them. We’re committed to working with this ecosystem so firms can bring their own expertise, standards, and judgment to AI—and serve clients in ways only they can.

To explore early access to Astra for Law, build it into your product, or develop tools around your firm’s expertise, contact OpenAI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cooley’s GO Public offering uses ChatGPT Work to surface complications earlier, focus expertise, and help clients reach market faster.

Cooley is an international law firm with a reputation for helping companies navigate capital markets and initial public offerings (IPOs). In 2025, the firm advised on 180 deals globally, totaling more than $51.5 billion in deal volume. Cooley has a decade-long track record at the top of the US issuer-side IPO market and has advised on more venture-backed IPOs than any other firm over the past 20-plus years.

Capital markets involve huge amounts of information that need to be synthesized and analyzed. “For our lawyers, it’s always very busy,” explains David Wang, Chief Innovation Officer at Cooley. “When there’s an IPO, there are thousands of things that need to be done constantly.”.

According to recent reports, cooley developed GO Public, a proprietary AI product offering built on ChatGPT Work. Its agentic harness analyzes information so lawyers can review and validate the work. The workflow comes together into a tailored starting point for an IPO.

“An IPO is one of the most consequential moments in a firm’s life, and it can consume enormous management attention,” states Dave Peinsipp, partner and co-chair of Cooley’s global capital markets group. “GO Public helps us move through the intensive preparation faster so lawyers and management teams can spend more time on the decisions that shape the transaction — where judgment, market experience and strategic thinking matter most.”.

Recent findings suggest that before GO Public, teams often began with a precedent from a comparable organization and adapted it to fit the client’s circumstances. GO Public allows Cooley to begin with the client itself, bringing together the information provided, relevant public sources, and carefully curated precedents to create a more tailored starting point for lawyer review.

“Everybody understands that as the leading capital markets firm, we know what to do in an IPO,” Wang states. Cooley’s legal engineers, innovation counsel, and practitioners worked together to translate the firm’s capital markets experience into a proprietary agentic system. “With GO Public and the agentic harness that we built using OpenAI’s technology, we were able to bring this forward into the AI era,” Wang says.

It has been revealed that the harness provides a controlled workflow for agents that lays out which steps agents can perform automatically, where lawyers must review or validate the work, and how it all comes together. Information curated from previous analyses provides what Wang calls “baked-in know-how.” Cooley partners closely with OpenAI to combine subject-matter expertise and AI engineering knowledge to ensure the right processes produce the right outcomes.

With GO Public, Cooley can redirect more lawyer and management time toward the substantive work that drives an IPO. “The amazing thing about integrating ChatGPT Work into GO Public is that it brings intelligence to this very large array of information that had to be manually sorted before,” Wang says. “Once you do that first cut, you’re able to really concentrate the human effort and expertise on the highest value surface areas.”.

According to recent reports, “That’s what we mean by speed to quality,” Peinsipp states. “The point isn’t simply to do the same work faster. It’s to get to a strong starting point sooner, so our lawyers can spend more time applying judgment, challenging the disclosure and thinking strategically about the problems that matter most to the firm.”.

For management teams, the benefit extends beyond the legal work itself. IPO preparation competes for the attention of executives who are also running fast-moving businesses.

Industry observers note that “Traditionally, the legal industry has been relatively change-averse,” Wang indicates. But AI is giving Cooley an opportunity to rethink how capital markets work gets done while preserving the professional judgment and accountability clients depend on.

It has been revealed that “As attorneys, we have professional duties and obligations to make sure that the best, most legally defensible outcome occurs for our clients, and that just takes a lot of work,” Wang explains. GO Public, powered by OpenAI, is designed to help lawyers consider more information while directing their expertise toward the decisions that matter most.

Peinsipp sees GO Public as the beginning of a broader shift in how capital markets work is delivered.

Industry observers note that “GO Public is our vision for the future of capital markets practice,” Peinsipp indicates. “Our collaboration with OpenAI has allowed us to rethink how this work gets done. We see enormous potential not only for IPOs but for capital markets transactions more broadly.”.

#28695. Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1668 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse.
  • Industry observers note that other disciplines test differently.
  • In a recent development, data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Software Engineer, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

Technical Lead, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Recent findings suggest that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse. Ideally, you'd develop and test it against production data, but access restrictions and data sensitivity make that difficult – especially when the engineers building the agent sit outside the team that owns the data. Even with access, a live warehouse is a poor test track: Catalog descriptions are often incomplete or contradicted by institutional knowledge in docs and chat threads; there’s no verified answer key across its thousands of tables; and you can't systematically vary the complexity of the data and documents to see where the agent breaks. So teams often test on toy datasets and hope the agent holds up in production.

Industry observers note that other disciplines test differently. Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges. A shape that performs well in the tunnel performs well on the road because the tunnel preserves the physical properties the shape responds to.

In a recent development, data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document. It is designed to preserve what the agent reasons over: how tables relate, what business events create which records, where institutional knowledge lives, and how definitions get messy. When those properties hold, an agent's behavior in the tunnel tracks its behavior on production data, even though the two share no sensitive content.

Sources indicate that at Google, we built an internal data simulator to serve as a wind tunnel for our enterprise data agents. Rather than copying proprietary schemas or cataloging every undocumented quirk in a live warehouse, an engineer starts with a short, plain-English description of organizational patterns, for example: "Simulate a two-plant brake manufacturer with an ERP, a shop-floor execution system, and a three-shift schedule where second-shift supervisors track downtime differently from operations and finance." From just a few sentences, the simulator invents a structurally analogous company ("Calder Brakes"), generating its schemas, rows, event history, documents, and chat threads alongside a benchmark of hard questions and a verified answer key.

Figure 1. Production data and its synthetic counterpart share causal structure without sharing sensitive content. A short description of domain patterns seeds the wind tunnel, where the agent is evaluated over read-only tools and behavioral trends carry back to production.

It has been revealed that why did we do this? Most data agents are evaluated on small, clean test databases with well-labeled tables, unambiguous metrics, and no conflicting documents. Those datasets are convenient, but they rarely test the judgment that enterprise data demands.

It has been revealed that once generated, a synthetic estate is served through a read-only interface — SQL execution, schema browsing, and document search — that any agent can call without seeing the blueprint or answer key. But consider what happens when an agent is asked either a qualitative onboarding question or a quantitative metric question from our simulated factory, "Calder Brakes Plant 2":.

It has been revealed that qualitative: "A new analyst is joining the team. What should they know about how 'downtime' is handled here, before they start producing reports?".

Recent findings suggest that A naive agent falls into the same trap on both questions. It searches for the most authoritative document and finds a policy memo from Bob, a second-shift supervisor, which states that downtime means unplanned stoppages only, and planned changeovers don't count. Bob is confident, articulate, and senior, so the agent summarizes his definition — and filters out planned changeovers when writing its SQL query.

Both answers are wrong. In fact, the plant's official metric counts changeovers as planned downtime. Bob sincerely believes his version because it flatters his shift's numbers, but weeks later the metric owner quietly corrects the record in a follow-up thread. Getting either question right requires looking past a document's tone, checking who owns the metric before writing SQL, and tracing later corrections. This is where data agents often fail in production.

According to recent reports, A synthetic estate is only useful for evaluation if its answer key is accurate and reproducible. Our simulator achieves this by separating simulated organization’s design from data generation across four stages (Figure 2).

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. One pipeline, one source of truth. In the estate-generation pipeline, only ① Compile blueprint invents facts and ③ Render documents phrases those fixed facts as prose (blue boxes); ② Simulate & build tables (plus SQL answer computation) runs deterministically from the frozen blueprint and seed, before ④ Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

In a recent development, first, the Compile blueprint stage uses a language model to turn the pattern prompt into a frozen blueprint specifying the firm's systems, people, metrics, and individual beliefs. Those beliefs can be mistaken on purpose — Bob's flawed definition of downtime is recorded alongside the official metric, planting the trap and its solution together.

Industry observers note that in the estate-generation pipeline, Compile blueprint is the only point where a language model decides what is true. Once the blueprint is frozen, Simulate & build tables runs deterministically without a model: employees act on their schedules, triggering tickets, shift handovers, and database rows, so that every record traces back to the event that created it. Organizational messiness emerges naturally from this timeline, such as outdated procedures or conflicting definitions, while row-level flaws that model real ingestion glitches (e.g., retry-storm duplicate rows, unmerged keys, or a mid-quarter unit change) are injected into the tables. Every flaw is recorded in a machine-readable messiness log so the benchmark generator can adjust the ground-truth SQL queries to account for the messy tables.

Recent findings suggest that given the same blueprint and random seed, the simulator produces identical tables and an identical SQL answer key on every run. The only subsequent step in building the estate that calls a model is Render documents, which turns the facts fixed in the blueprint into memos and chat threads in each person's writing style. Finally, Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

Three build-time checks keep the benchmark honest:.

Computed SQL and rubric gold answers: Every quantitative question ships with the SQL query that computes its expected ("gold") answer against the messy tables. Because the messiness log records injected retry duplicates on defect rows, the benchmark generator automatically pairs a defect-count question with the deduplicating COUNT(DISTINCT) query (240) – and runs decoy SQL queries representing common mistakes (like an un-deduplicated COUNT(*) or Bob's changeover filter) to verify that falling for a trap yields a different number. Qualitative questions ship with a rubric grounded in the blueprint's metric owner, official definition, and correction trail. If the estate lacks the data to verify a question, the generator drops the item rather than shipping an unverified question.

Verified documents: Every rendered memo and chat thread is checked against the blueprint to confirm it states its assigned facts without introducing unrecorded numbers, dates, or names.

Hallucination sentinels: The simulator plants questions about invented metrics like "Basalt Velocity Ratio" that appear nowhere in the estate; a reliable agent abstains and reports that no such metric exists.

A wind tunnel does not need to match the exact score an agent gets on production data; it needs to reproduce the same behavioral trends: direction (if longer reasoning chains lower accuracy on real data, they should lower accuracy in the tunnel) and rate (accuracy should degrade at the similar pace as contradictions accumulate). When those trends hold, you can confidently compare agent versions and dial up complexity step by step to find where reasoning breaks down.

We test how closely our simulated estates match reality — and whether evaluation signals carry over — at three levels:.

Our simulator builds on two research threads. In database question answering, benchmarks like BIRD and Spider 2.0 have moved from clean schemas to messy databases, while agent environments like WebArena, tool-use benchmarks like τ-bench, and Generative Agents simulate websites or use language models to role-play human people. In contrast, our simulator's employees follow deterministic rules tied to their roles and schedules, so a single seed replays the exact same organizational history every time.

We also adapt an intuition from domain randomization in robotics, where simulations vary surface details like lighting and textures during training while keeping the underlying physics faithful. Applied to data agent evaluation, that means synthesizing every surface name, number, and document from a short pattern description, while keeping the causal structure, cross-document links, and institutional messiness faithful to enterprise reality.

It has been revealed that generating a test estate on demand removes a bottleneck between enterprises that own sensitive data, and the engineering teams building data agents for them. Traditionally, developing and benchmarking an enterprise agent required access to production tables and a hand-labeled question set — the two assets hardest to share across organizational or compliance boundaries. We use this wind tunnel internally to stress-test and harden Google Cloud's data agents against realistic enterprise messiness without touching customer data, and the same blueprint-first architecture can be applied by any engineering team building evaluation suites for their own agents.

According to recent reports, synthetic evaluation still carries two risks: overfitting to the simulator's patterns of messiness, and drift as a live business evolves away from its blueprint. The discipline required is the same one that wind-tunnel engineers practice: Periodically calibrate the tunnel against real-world runs, keep benchmark difficulty aligned with production failure modes, and treat the simulation as a living model. Your agents — and their owners — will thank you.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI’s approach to protecting, empowering, and creating safer experiences for young people.
  • We are introducing the Australian Youth Safety Blueprint⁠(opens in a new window), a roadmap for protecting young people as they use AI and a practical contribution to the Australian policy landscape.
  • It has been revealed that we are continuing to strengthen safeguards in our products, informed by these principles.

OpenAI’s approach to protecting, empowering, and creating safer experiences for young people.

We are introducing the Australian Youth Safety Blueprint⁠(opens in a new window), a roadmap for protecting young people as they use AI and a practical contribution to the Australian policy landscape. Young Australians deserve tools that expand their opportunities to learn, create, and build skills while protecting their wellbeing. The Blueprint sets out six pillars, from AI literacy and age-appropriate safeguards to privacy-protective age assurance, connections to real-world crisis support, and accessible parental controls. Together, they help define how responsible AI should work for teens, and how companies should be held accountable for identifying and addressing risks to young people.

It has been revealed that we are continuing to strengthen safeguards in our products, informed by these principles. In August, we began rolling out ChatGPT for Teens in Australia, a upcoming default experience for users identified as aged 13 to 17, with updated safeguards designed around their developmental needs. This builds on our parental controls, under-18 safety policies, and age assurance, which helps apply the right protections to the right users. The responsibility for safety should not fall primarily on young people or their families. Companies must continue to build protections into their products from the outset.

This is ongoing work, and there is more to do. Australia has an opportunity to help shape strong, evidence-based standards that protect young people while preserving access to the benefits of AI. We are committed to learning alongside teens, parents, educators, researchers, and policymakers, and we welcome collaboration from others working towards the same goal.

📅 21 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1168 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

V7 cuts costs 78% while boosting accuracy with GPT-5.6 Luna

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How V7 gives AI agents institutional memory for complex work, with GPT‑6 Astra hitting 89% accuracy on its hardest graph-query tests.
  • Today’s models can reason through complex tasks, but they don’t automatically understand the underlying business context of those tasks.
  • It has been revealed that that context lives in documents, data rooms, spreadsheets, emails, and internal tools: scattered, unresolved, and invisible to agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How V7 gives AI agents institutional memory for complex work, with GPT‑6 Astra hitting 89% accuracy on its hardest graph-query tests.

Accuracy for GPT-6 Astra on the hardest queries.

Lower cost per document with GPT-5.6 Luna.

Higher accuracy with GPT-5.6 Luna.

Today’s models can reason through complex tasks, but they don’t automatically understand the underlying business context of those tasks. Which fund report is current? How is the same entity named across three systems?

It has been revealed that that context lives in documents, data rooms, spreadsheets, emails, and internal tools: scattered, unresolved, and invisible to agents. For teams in finance, insurance, and real estate, retrieval accuracy within workflows is non-negotiable.

It has been revealed that after building a widely used computer vision accessibility app together, Rizzoli and Edwardsson started V7⁠(opens in a fresh window) in 2018 to help companies teach AI systems how their businesses work. V7 Go is an agentic platform to build mission critical workflows, and organize buried context into memory that agents can query and act on.

V7 Go uses GPT‑5.6 Luna to extract information from millions of files and organize it in the Context Graph, which connects entities, relationships, and cited evidence, powering MCP search and repeatable workflows that can span hundreds of steps. For Workflows, V7 Go uses GPT‑5.6 Terra and Sol for reasoning and tool use across complex, multi-step instructions that take humans dozens of hours to complete. V7 is also starting to use GPT‑6 Astra on the most demanding Context Graph queries, including financial analysis across thousands of documents.

With context, models, and tools working together, V7 notes agents complete 50–100 step workflows in minutes, reaching 99.9% accuracy, while maintaining an auditable trail of every decision made.

Industry observers note that the Context Graph solves a specific problem. Agents have to rediscover context on every request, leading to dozens of searches costing time and tokens, and often missing key information buried in relationships.

When data arrives, V7 Go connects to repositories such as SharePoint and Google Drive, scans them for entities, relationships, facts, attributes, and metrics, and populates a graph that’s an order of magnitude cheaper and faster to traverse than long-context approaches.

The Context Graph gives agents a structured, up-to-date record they can query directly. When a new file arrives, V7 Go identifies the companies, funds, people, or any entity in an ontology, then connects each fact to a new or existing record, and preserves cited evidence to the original source. If the graph does not contain enough information, V7 Go can still search the underlying documents with RAG.

V7 has also tested how much the structure of that context matters. On HERB, a benchmark for finding and connecting information spread across enterprise systems, V7’s retrieval-only system outperformed the official baseline by 69% and reduced hallucinations on un-answerable queries by 38%. V7 Go uses that source-linked context to keep complex workflows grounded in each firm’s own information.

According to recent reports, V7 Go uses that organized context in workflows such as private equity deal screening and insurance underwriting. In the demo below, a workflow extracts information from a deal document called a Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM) feeds key financials, deal terms, management details, and cites risk fields before V7 Go produces a screening note.

The Context Graph makes it so that a model can work with a firm’s history without relearning it each time. For long-running agents, V7 Go keeps recent exchanges in the model’s active context and stores older material in the graph to be retrieved when needed.

That shared context is already speeding up document-heavy work across V7’s customers:.

Asset managers can screen deals 21x faster than before, reducing a full-day process to just 15 minutes.

A financial services team cut review time from more than 100 hours to under 10, saving $12,000 in expert costs per task.

Insurance teams reduced errors in claims processing by 13.5% compared to a manual baseline, after granting their agents historical knowledge of all previous claims and existing policies.

Sources indicate that complex, multi-step workflows depend on a model reliably following lengthy instructions, running tools, interpreting results, and navigating a long series of steps. A single upstream error can lead to expensive consequences and broken trust in AI systems. V7 Go guides models across long horizon tasks spanning deterministic code, handovers to smaller models, file generation steps, and integrations, with an auditable trace of every run.

In AI-generated workflows, V7 Go maps each step to fast, medium, and smart tiers. GPT‑5.6 Luna handles structured extraction and other high-volume work, and GPT‑5.6 Terra or Sol power chat, the Go Agent path, and steps that require more reasoning or tool use.

Recent findings suggest that V7 tests fresh models against a continuously maintained benchmark suite covering citation accuracy, extraction quality across hundreds of document types, answer correctness, instruction following, latency, cost, and real-world enterprise workflows. OpenAI outperforms most models on the behaviors V7 cares about most. OpenAI also approved and implemented V7’s capacity increase needs within hours, compared with weeks for other providers V7 uses.

In V7’s latest harness, key workflows with several external calls now finish up to 50% faster. V7 measured another efficiency gain with GPT‑5.6 Luna: a 78% lower cost per document than with GPT‑5.4 mini. V7 also moved its document-heavy V7 Go workloads from the Chat Completions API to the Responses API. In its testing, the change reduced token use by roughly 5% for some PDF-heavy workflows and improved caching reliability.

Recent findings suggest that V7 also tested GPT‑6 Astra on its most difficult queries. GPT‑5.6 Sol had saturated many of V7’s existing benchmarks, so the tech giant created a more challenging set of graph-query questions using messier, real-world data across thousands of documents. The test’s dataset spans four difficulty levels. On the very-hard level, V7 reports that GPT‑5.6 Sol scored 78%, while GPT‑6 Astra scored 89% accuracy. Both models scored close to 100% on the easy, medium, and hard levels.

Industry observers note that V7 Go already exposes Context Graph querying and ingestion through its MCP server, so customers can use it from ChatGPT and other compatible clients. They can also create V7 Go workflows through MCP in Codex. Together with simpler workflow design, this has reduced the time required to create a medium-length workflow from around one hour to about 20 minutes.

V7’s longer-term goal is to make that shared memory more proactive. The team is working toward workflows that start when facts in the Context Graph change, flag inconsistencies, and show people which analyses need another look. A restated fund report, for example, could prompt V7 Go to flag work that still relies on the old figures.

Sources indicate that “Our goal is to help enterprises re-tool for the age of AI, with workflows that solve mission critical tasks, and memory that outperforms us humans” notes Rizzoli. “Finance firms getting real value from AI will not be the ones with the most agents. They will be the ones with the best context.”.

Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cogent combines OpenAI models with enterprise context to help automatically remediate vulnerabilities with agents.
  • As Cogent Security⁠(opens in a new window) sees enterprises facing more security risks than ever, it has found that the hardest part is not finding vulnerabilities, but fixing them.
  • Cogent builds Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises to autonomously find and eliminate those risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cogent combines OpenAI models with enterprise context to help automatically remediate vulnerabilities with agents.

Lower mean time to remediate vulnerabilities.

As Cogent Security⁠(opens in a new window) sees enterprises facing more security risks than ever, it has found that the hardest part is not finding vulnerabilities, but fixing them. Remediation work is complex and spans multiple teams. It requires contextual understanding of a organization’s environment: how could an attacker exploit a vulnerability, which business systems are at stake, and what changes can be made safely.

Cogent builds Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises to autonomously find and eliminate those risks. The factories are designed to help defenders move at machine speed, in response to the acceleration in vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

The manufacturer’s AI agents combine GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑5.6 with its enterprise context and controls to handle investigation through verified remediation. The agents assess exposures, execute permitted changes, and confirm the risk has been eliminated. Cogent also conducts internal research with Cyber and Daybreak, exploring attack paths and defensive capabilities.

For each customer, Cogent’s Context Engine maintains an enterprise knowledge graph of assets, vulnerabilities, identities, ownership, and dependencies. Specialized background agents continuously reconcile information across security tools and systems, giving investigation and remediation agents a shared understanding of the environment.

Recent findings suggest that GPT‑6 Astra handles upfront planning and complex reasoning for that work. This enables what Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO of Cogent, describes as a “memory harness for the enterprise.” He says, “We don’t have to relearn what the world looks like every time a newly introduced task happens.” Reusing context reduces latency, inference costs, and inconsistent results.

Cogent’s Agent Policies define each enterprise’s permitted changes and approval requirements, and its policy-enforcement engine, TRACE, checks tool calls against the policies before execution. The checks are deterministic and require no separate model inference.

According to recent reports, an Agent Gateway independently checks authorization, and higher-risk work can run in isolated sandboxes. Customers can delegate investigation, require approval for changes, or permit bounded autonomous remediation.

When critical security flaws known as PHP2Shell were disclosed in PHP, a programming language used to run websites, customers turned to the Cyber Defense Factories that Cogent had already deployed in their environments.

GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Astra provided the deep reasoning for investigation and remediation planning. Using Cogent’s context layer, agents identified affected systems, assessed exposure, and developed looks that accounted for application dependencies and operational constraints. Then they orchestrated fixes using customer-defined approval and execution workflows and verified the resolution.

Cogent reports that customers are using its Cyber Defense Factories to resolve vulnerabilities faster and expand investigation capacity. With Cogent, a Fortune 1000 automotive customer reduced its mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities by 75%, and a Fortune 500 IT services customer achieved 5× vulnerability-triage throughput.

Global electronic trading platform MarketAxess leverages Cogent to help strengthen its risk-based approach to exposure management. “Cogent brings together vulnerability data, business context, security controls, and attack path analysis to help us validate real exposures and prioritize remediation where it matters most. What stands out is how rapidly the Cogent team responds to emerging threats and turns our feedback into practical capabilities,” says Vijay Bala, CISO, MarketAxess.

Recent findings suggest that cogent continuously evaluates closed-source and open-source alternatives and reports stronger reasoning on long-running security tasks, higher fidelity, fewer hallucinations on technical codebases, and more reliable execution with OpenAI models. The models can chain tool calls sequentially and in parallel while retaining context across remediation workflows.

In a recent development, cogent prioritizes reasoning quality for complex investigations and cost for more straightforward work. It uses GPT‑6.1 Sol for general execution and GPT‑5.6 for routine vulnerability-management tasks where advanced reasoning is less critical.

It has been revealed that using OpenAI models has also reduced the supporting software Cogent needs to build for remediation and patching. “A lot of the work that we had to do at the harness level is no longer required,” Geng notes. He also shared that OpenAI APIs have “streamlined request routing and agent orchestration, significantly reducing internal engineering overhead and accelerating our time-to-market for complex security workflows.”.

Most of Cogent’s engineers also choose Codex for development. Geng indicates they’re more productive pairing Codex with OpenAI models vs. using the same models in an open-source coding environment. “Codex just comes with tools that we don’t have to build ourselves,” says Geng.

Through Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak, Cogent receives technical support for its internal red-teaming and attack-path research. Daybreak Red, an access tier within Daybreak, provides the team with specialized OpenAI models for authorized offensive and vulnerability research. “Good defense requires good offense,” Geng states.

According to recent reports, cogent intends to expand its capabilities as the key partner for enterprises to build their own Cyber Defense Factories. Its roadmap includes increasingly autonomous remediation, broadening the range and complexity of fixes agents can execute, from straightforward configuration changes to multi-step workflows spanning different enterprise systems.

Recent findings suggest that the organization is also developing autonomous discovery and validation. Its goal is a closed-loop system that finds and eliminates risk while continuously learning from every vulnerability to improve future investigations and fixes.

Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.
  • Recent findings suggest that for freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a fresh skill or expands a project’s scope.
  • Upwork’s 2026 Future Workforce Index⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) found that 38% of skilled U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.

Recent findings suggest that for freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a fresh skill or expands a project’s scope. Our new research with Upwork offers an early view of these changes in the AI era. Some familiar services are losing market share, while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities—and involve larger budgets and more hours of work.

The stakes are substantial. Upwork’s 2026 Future Workforce Index⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) found that 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance. Its previous annual study⁠(opens in a new window) estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. Those estimates extend well beyond Upwork’s own marketplace.

Freelance work can also reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics. Contracts are often short, and clients can adjust their requirements with each posting. To get to the root of these changes, we partnered with Upwork, an online marketplace connecting clients and freelancers, to study those requests alongside the activities people undertake directly with ChatGPT.

The mix of work differed across the two platforms. Writing accounted for a much larger share of ChatGPT use, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of requests for freelancers in Upwork postings.

Below are the ranges of tasks between the two platforms.

These activities represent only the largest changes in Upwork shares over the studied period. ChatGPT shares cover Jan 2025–Jun 2026; Upwork shares are H1 2026. Changes in Upwork share are H1 2025 to H1 2026, in percentage points.

According to recent reports, many activities that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share on Upwork, while less common activities gained share. Of the 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed this pattern.

Sources indicate that the remaining 20 work categories highlighted the reverse. ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand.

The comparison also captures how people presently use ChatGPT, not the full range of tasks AI can support—a gap OpenAI calls the capability overhang.

Recent findings suggest that each point represents one of 63 matched work subcategories in the Upwork taxonomy. The horizontal axis is the natural log of the category’s share of ChatGPT use in H2 2025 divided by its share of Upwork job posts in H1 2023. The vertical axis shows the percentage change in the category’s share of Upwork postings from H1 2023 to H2 2025, on a logarithmic scale; 0% indicates unchanged marketplace share. The vertical divider at AI intensity 0 marks equal category shares in ChatGPT and baseline Upwork postings.

It has been revealed that by late 2025, clients were requesting the use of AI in many more, different kinds of work. Clients were seeking freelancers to apply AI in tasks including chatbot development, video production, marketing automation, and application integration.

Within individual projects, AI capabilities were often requested alongside other work. AI-related postings listed about as many tasks as other postings but more often combined tasks that had rarely appeared together in earlier jobs.

Some clients asked for AI-generated video, editing, and motion graphics in a single posting. The freelancer would bring those skills together to deliver a finished video.

Between early 2023 and late 2025, the mix of tasks in AI-related postings became 45% more diverse—the equivalent of an increase from about 15 equally common tasks to about 21.

Although posted hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work. This pattern suggests that higher budgets may partly reflect a broader scope of work.

It has been revealed that AI’s effects on work can be difficult to detect in employment statistics. As we have noted in previous Work at the Frontier papers, the effects may appear first in the work people do.

Because freelance projects turn over quickly, postings are continually refreshed as clients’ needs change. Work within firms can evolve without appearing in a latest job posting. Combined with ChatGPT data, these postings offer an early view of which activities people undertake directly with AI, which they hire freelancers to perform, and how AI-related projects differ from other work.

According to recent reports, the findings do not point to a simple substitution story. Some activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, but this pattern was not uniform. AI-related work also spanned a wider mix of activities, combined tasks in less familiar ways, and carried larger fixed-price budgets and more hours. Together, these patterns suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects.

The OpenAI Economic Research Team explores how AI is changing work in real time with the Work at the Frontier series.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the OpenAI API and models, Singapore Airlines improves customer support, travel discovery, and employee work, doubling CSAT for the Kris customer service chatbot.

Increase in customer satisfaction score (CSAT) with AI-powered Kris chatbot.

Reduction in average handling time for customer service representatives using AI-assisted tools.

Growth in Flight Recommender monthly users over the past year.

Industry observers note that AI is becoming part of how Singapore Airlines serves customers, empowers employees, and builds technology. The airline uses the OpenAI API for customer-facing experiences and OpenAI models inside Jarvis, its governed internal AI platform for employees. It also uses OpenAI models in its software development workflows to deliver more personalized service, improve productivity, and help teams build more efficiently.

Across these deployments, Singapore Airlines pairs OpenAI models with orchestration, internal data controls, validation, and human review, giving teams a consistent way to bring AI into production workflows responsibly.

According to recent reports, one of Singapore Airlines’ most visible AI applications is Kris, its customer-facing chatbot. After moving Kris from a traditional dialog-flow system to an LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API, Singapore Airlines saw a 2x increase in customer satisfaction.

Recent findings suggest that alongside that, the airline deployed AI-assisted tools for customer service representatives, including OpenAI API-powered call summarization, so that representatives spend less time on after-call work and more time on the customer. Singapore Airlines saw an approximately 10% reduction in average handling time for its customer service representatives.

In the earlier dialog-flow based chatbot design, every topic had to be mapped manually, and every flow had to be written in advance. That made coverage difficult to scale. If an intent was missing, the conversation was more likely to end up requiring support from a customer service representative, even when the customer’s request could have been handled through self-service.

Industry observers note that singapore Airlines moved Kris to a fully LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API. Instead of depending on predefined flows, the chatbot can interpret customer intent in natural language, ground answers in a knowledge base, manage multi-topic conversations, and hand over to a customer service representative with the relevant context when needed.

Recent findings suggest that today, customers use Kris for general queries, special requests, real-time flight disruption information, and selected transactional workflows. Singapore Airlines is continuing to expand its capabilities to include booking changes, baggage transactions, and more complex agentic interactions.

Flight Recommender lets customers describe the trip they want in natural language instead of repeatedly adjusting filters, dates, and destinations. Usage has grown nearly 3x over the past year.

Built on the OpenAI API, Flight Recommender uses an orchestration layer connected to fare and availability data. It interprets customer intent, calls the relevant tools, and returns personalized travel recommendations in natural language.

Industry observers note that the team has also implemented guardrails for input and output validation, malicious or inappropriate query handling, hallucination reduction, PII handling, and authenticated access to only the context required for each query. Singapore Airlines is preparing to expand the experience into a more conversational chatbot interaction, where customers can keep refining travel ideas rather than restarting a search.

Beyond customer-facing experiences, Singapore Airlines is also using OpenAI models in parts of the software development lifecycle to help teams plan, refine, test, and review work more efficiently. Across selected software development lifecycle activities, teams have achieved productivity gains of up to 20%.

Recent findings suggest that AI now runs through the entire delivery lifecycle and not just coding. Teams use generative AI models to support requirements refinement, stakeholder-session analysis, product specifications, edge-case identification, test-case creation, architecture review, and the breakdown of complex work into smaller, more testable tasks.

For one commercial feature, the team used the OpenAI API to challenge assumptions, identify ambiguous requirements and surface edge cases before development begins. Once those were well-defined, AI helped translate them into design options, implementation looks, test cases and then code generation.

According to recent reports, during deployment and beyond, AI also helps to interpret how the system is behaving in production, and flagging issues that might otherwise go unnoticed. With AI active at every step of the workflow, team members have shifted from producing every artifact themselves, to directing, reviewing and validating what AI produces throughout the delivery lifecycle. This means they can focus on work that truly requires human judgement, such as prioritization, architecture, governance and stakeholder outcomes.

Sources indicate that more broadly, OpenAI models are helping Singapore Airlines improve requirements quality, test coverage, and conformance with internal standards. Teams use these workflows to generate edge cases for testing, review architecture aims, and support human validation before work moves further through the development lifecycle.

According to recent reports, beyond engineering teams, Singapore Airlines is making AI accessible across the business through Jarvis, its internal AI platform. Powered by OpenAI models, Jarvis gives employees a governed way to use AI in their day-to-day work, from summarizing documents to creating custom workflows.

It has been revealed that employees use Jarvis to work across PDFs, Word documents, Excel files, PowerPoint decks, and other file types in a secure environment, while creating custom workflows and lightweight knowledge bases for their day-to-day work. Today, more than 60% of Singapore Airlines employees are using Jarvis monthly with adoption continuing to increase.

2x increase in customer satisfaction score (CSAT) after changing to AI-based Kris chatbot.

~10% reduction in average handling time for customer service agents using AI-assisted tools.

3x growth in monthly consumers of Flight Recommender, its customer-facing travel discovery tool, over the past year.

Singapore Airlines is continuing to expand AI across customer and employee workflows. For Kris, the next phase is deeper self-service, with more transactional capabilities that help customers resolve requests directly in chat. Flight Recommender is moving toward a more conversational travel discovery experience, where customers can refine ideas over multiple turns rather than restarting a search.

With Jarvis available across the business, Singapore Airlines is focused on helping more employees put AI to work in their day-to-day roles. Closing the AI guidance gap in education

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Drawing on upcoming ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.
  • AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for.
  • Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Drawing on upcoming ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.

AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for. As intelligence becomes easier to access and apply, the question is no longer simply what people need to know, but which skills and capabilities will help them thrive in an AI-enabled world. Recent debates around PISA and AI, including those led by the OECD’s Andreas Schleicher⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), underscore this shift. They also point to a central lesson: as AI becomes more capable, the role of teachers becomes more important, not less. Their expertise, judgement and ability to guide learning remain essential. Equipping teachers, schools and governments with AI skills and confidence to make informed decisions about these tools must therefore be a priority for education systems.

Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators. These collaborations share three priorities: equitable access to frontier AI tools, jointly designed AI literacy programmes, and ongoing measurement and evaluation, whilst adapting to local languages, curricula and institutions.

It has been revealed that this report shares emerging lessons from our education partnerships in EMEA, focusing on educator support, AI literacy, local capability and evaluation. It examines what partners have tried, what they have reported and what remains uncertain. Country examples reflect their particular contexts and arrangements, and their findings should be interpreted within those limits. Five themes organise these lessons: clear educational goals, educator preparation, local partnerships, critical AI literacy and credible evidence.

Three early patterns are emerging from this work:.

Industry observers note that country partnerships offer context-specific lessons. Experiences in Estonia, Greece and Slovakia point to three lessons that other education systems can apply: strong public leadership to set a clear direction, investment in teachers' skills and confidence, and practical support tailored to local curricula and classroom needs. While implementation will vary across countries, these principles offer a useful foundation for governments seeking to integrate AI responsibly and at scale.

According to recent reports, closing the AI guidance gap in education is becoming increasingly urgent. New research from ThinkYoung,⁠(opens in a new window) which examines the ways teachers and students are already engaging with AI highlights a clear guidance gap: 79% of surveyed students reported using AI for homework or assignments, but only 47% reported being shown how. Governments need to support educators and give students clearer expectations. Below we set out how educators can be better supported to set the terms and conditions of use.

Early benefits for teachers are clear. Adoption and reported time savings for teachers are encouraging. Understanding where AI strengthens knowledge, independent thinking and retention requires sustained evaluation and through the government actions that we observed, we identify how to prioritise more research into this critical area.

Industry observers note that our aim is to share practical lessons from these partnerships that education leaders can consider in their own contexts. These are early experiences, rather than a single model for education systems to follow.

It has been revealed that we are also learning how to judge progress with evidence: teacher adoption and reported time savings offer encouraging early signals. Surveys, programme monitoring and consultation help us understand participants’ experiences and the barriers they encounter.

Sources indicate that at OpenAI, our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits everyone. Helping learners flourish is central to that ambition. We believe that every young person should have the opportunity to develop the skills to participate in a world increasingly shaped by AI, whatever their background or wherever they attend school. We have a responsibility to contribute to that evidence and learn openly from the findings, including when they challenge our assumptions. Through the OpenAI Learning Lab, we are bringing education researchers together to understand when and how AI can support education systems.

Recent findings suggest that the choices made today will shape how the next generation learns, works and participates in society. With ambition, care, public leadership and a commitment to evidence, AI can help extend educational opportunity and strengthen young people’s capacity to understand, create and act for themselves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claim your business, keep your information current, and understand how people engage with you in ChatGPT.

Patch on November 19, 2026: Ecommerce and online service businesses based outside the U.S. are now eligible to claim their business and publish agents in ChatGPT.

Originally published on November 10, 2026.

Industry observers note that we’re introducing Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a new way to connect with the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. Through Business Hub⁠(opens in a new window), businesses can claim their business, manage their information, and see insights on how people engage with them on ChatGPT. In addition, we are adding a powerful new way for businesses to interact with owners via Business Agents, starting with eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S.

Industry observers note that together, these products create more ways for businesses to connect with people as they explore options and make decisions. They strengthen how people discover and interact with businesses in ChatGPT through broader business coverage, up-to-date information, and the ability to connect with a business through its Business Agent. Throughout these experiences, protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT remains our North Star.

Recent findings suggest that in Business Hub, companies can claim their organization in ChatGPT and, once verified, update key details and add self-service product feeds with pricing and availability. This gives businesses a new way to provide information to ChatGPT, helping people explore products and services using the most accurate and up-to-date details.

Recent findings suggest that any eligible business located where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in ChatGPT through Business Hub. Existing OpenAI Enterprise customers and advertisers can work directly with their OpenAI representative to claim their business. Shopify merchants can connect their store from Business Hub or the Shopify admin to streamline verification. Eligible products from Shopify merchants are already integrated into ChatGPT through Shopify Catalog.

Business Hub provides aggregated insights into how people engage with a business in ChatGPT. This includes the number of mentions and website clicks a business receives. Businesses can also explore discovery topics—common themes across conversations where their website is cited. These insights can help businesses understand how they’re represented and find opportunities to improve the information they share.

We’ve designed these insights to protect user privacy. We don’t share users’ conversations or Business Agent chats with businesses. Insights are aggregated and are only available when there are enough conversations or interactions to meet certain thresholds.

After claiming their business in ChatGPT, eligible organizations can build, test, and launch a Business Agent—a new way to answer questions and help people explore their offerings.

Industry observers note that when a business appears in a model response, people can click to see the business’s ChatGPT profile. If a Business Agent is available, customers can choose to start a conversation with the business to explore its offerings and ask follow-up questions. For example, someone comparing products could ask about the differences between two options and which features fit their needs. A Business Agent could help them explore those questions using the business’s information.

For customers, this can make it easier to understand whether an offering is the right fit. For businesses, it creates a way to help interested customers learn more through a personalized conversation. The Business Agent conversation is clearly labeled, separate from the customer’s original ChatGPT conversation, and distinct from ChatGPT’s independent answers.

Businesses can also sponsor their Business Agent⁠ and use it as the destination for ChatGPT Ads to reach more potential customers. Sponsored placements are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT responses.

Business Agents are now available to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the United States. Learn more about eligible categories here⁠.

As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI. Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT. We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights, and conversations that help people make informed decisions. Over time, we plan to expand Businesses in ChatGPT and Business Agents to more markets and business categories, and build tools for organizations with more complex needs.

Sources indicate that as the platform evolves, we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers—directly or through agents—in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses new ways to participate and grow.

Learn more and⁠ claim your business in ChatGPT.⁠.
