📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.
  • Reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge.
  • To turn seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.

Reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge.

To turn seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context.

Saved on security code review with Codex.

According to recent reports, revolut⁠(opens in a fresh window) was built to challenge the way people interact with money. That ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets, 800,000 businesses and a consumer base that’s grown by 23% in the last 12 months.

Add to that a company culture that expects small, lean teams to move rapidly and it’s no surprise that ChatGPT and Codex have proven a natural fit.

“The perfect description for a high-caliber Revolut person is someone who can identify a problem really quickly, deduce the solution, design four scenarios, identify the best one of those four then take it to market,” states Kim Maniovich, Revolut’s Global Head of Business Marketing.

“Partnering with OpenAI enables us to build a lot of these solutions in a way that’s incredibly lean, cost-efficient and really tailored to the unique way that we work.”.

In a recent development, but moving faster is only part of the opportunity. For Revolut, the bigger question is what becomes possible when talented people spend less time on the mechanics of getting things done—and more time tackling problems that could fundamentally change financial services.

As Revolut grows, so does the complexity of protecting its customers. According to one report⁠(opens in a new window), over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025.

According to recent reports, for Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement robust and tailored protections for its customers. But the sheer volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank.

Recent findings suggest that “The biggest problem we can tackle with AI today is the scaling of humans versus the demand that we get,” indicates AI Lead David Abitbol. That’s why one of Revolut’s largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models.

Rather than requiring investigators to work through every eligible case manually, the agent can examine information, apply Revolut’s rules and complete the defined process automatically.

Industry observers note that the release of GPT‑5.5 was a turning point. It was then, notes Abitbol, that the models had become capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent. The result is greater capacity to monitor transactions without increasing investigator headcount at the same rate as demand.

That, adds Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri, “translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system our customers can trust.”.

‘Move fast but build trust’ could easily be Revolut’s internal engineering slogan. While Abitbol points out that Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, he’s also clear that certain guardrails are non-negotiable.

“We have a systematic framework where anyone in the firm who’s building anything with AI has the same set of standards across development, A/B testing, and business metric prediction,” he says. “So every engineer is held to the same standard of quality across the company. We started to get enough intelligence for reasonable costs where we could increasingly delegate initial investigations and screenings to the agent.”.

For Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik, that 30-60% reduction in coding time became tangible while he was building an internal code-review service. He designed the system, broke it into features and initially assumed he’d need a development team to implement it.

It has been revealed that “I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers to implement this,” he recalls. “I can just launch different agents and assign each of them a particular task.” Codex became his implementation team, while Dmitry spent more time designing the system, planning the work and reviewing what came back.

This is a pattern that Abitbol has seen across Revolut. As Codex returns capacity to engineers they’re using that reclaimed time “to spend more time discussing design and the best solution. So we spend more time designing instead of implementing.”.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t remove the need for engineering expertise, it just changes where that expertise is applied. “Every developer is responsible for the code they produce, and we don’t blindly trust AI,” Pitik says. The result is a different division of work: AI can help with implementation, while engineers devote more attention to the decisions that determine whether the software is useful, reliable and worth building.

Recent findings suggest that that overhead is worth it. As Codex works on one task, Pitik can work in parallel on another. That kind of multitasking is essential in a manufacturer where, as Kim Maniovich explains, the average employee has “three different jobs.” Using Codex creates a virtuous (if challenging) flywheel where “month on month the targets we’re setting get more aggressive, but also more attainable. And so the bar keeps moving up. AI is making that possible.”.

Examples of what Revolut has been able to do with this upcoming-found capacity include developing a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

According to recent reports, or turning seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context in a single day, creating a foundation for tools intended to help designers work more effectively. The exercise illustrates how AI can make accumulated organisational knowledge more accessible, reducing the effort required to work with complex systems. “We can shift focus from the things which are important but hard to do without AI to the things which matter for customers,” notes Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov.

Industry observers note that mo Amiri’s job is to make sure all of this speed is matched by security—not just for customers but for Revolut’s own employees. That gives him two views of AI at once: how it can help Revolut investigate a problem, and what teams need before they can deploy it safely.

In a phishing investigation, for example, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. “With stronger AI tools, we can uncover those connections instantly, and dig deeper into the questions that really matter,” he says.

While AI does the legwork and presents an investigator with a structured case, it’s still down to the individual to review the original records, decide whether the explanation makes sense and approve any action.

Amiri applies the same thinking when teams bring new AI applications into Revolut. He follows the complete chain: what information the system sees, where that information goes, which tools it can reach, what it can do with that access and what happens when something fails. He also tests whether apparently convincing conclusions are actually supported by the evidence.

According to recent reports, “The most critical decision is always about accountability,” he claims. “If an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand that change well enough to stand by it. That directly drives how we design the review process, giving developers the context they need without cluttering their everyday workflow.”.

Sources indicate that for Revolut, safeguards aren’t separate from innovation. They help establish the conditions under which teams can confidently adopt more capable technology. “That’s how you earn real confidence in AI,” he explains, “by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”.

30–60% reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge.

One engineer built an internal code-review service by delegating implementation tasks to multiple Codex agents.

One day to transform existing design-system documentation developed over roughly seven years into AI-readable context.

One to two days saved on one substantial security code-review task.

More transactions screened through the FinCrime agent without scaling investigators one for one.

Sources indicate that start with a problem worth solving. Revolut has put AI to work where demand is growing fastest and the stakes for customers are highest.

Industry observers note that use speed to raise ambition, not lower standards. Time saved on coding and investigation creates room for better design, harder questions and more consequential work.

Keep people on the hook. AI can gather evidence, write code and recommend action. A person still needs to understand the work well enough to stand behind it.

It has been revealed that build trust before you scale. Be clear about what a system can see, what it can do and what happens when it fails—then test those decisions as you go.

Make your knowledge usable. AI works better when it can reach clear, well-organised context. The same exercise often shows where the organisation itself needs to be clearer.

Revolut has already shown how AI can increase the amount and complexity of work its teams can attempt. Its next opportunity is to carry that combination of capability, judgment and design into the way customers interact with their money.

According to recent reports, abitbol imagines a more conversational interface in which customers can ask Revolut to help with everyday financial tasks: blocking a card, managing a subscription or finding ways to save for a trip. Pavlov sees the design challenge underneath that experience—turning complexity into something consistent, familiar and easy to use.

Recent findings suggest that kim Maniovich connects that future to the culture driving the work. “I hope that we can take the values that we operate by every day—this unapologetic ambition, the desire to never settle—and enable people to apply that to their own lives through the products that we build for them.”.

According to recent reports, as AI makes it easier to build, the differentiator becomes knowing what to build—and maintaining the judgment, standards and customer understanding to do it well. For Revolut, that’s the bigger promise of intelligence at work: less time spent on the mechanics of getting things done, and more capacity to make financial services safer, simpler and more useful for everyone.Banking services provided by licensed Revolut Group entities. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that how more than 1,800 scientists used ChatGPT—and what they expect AI to mean for scientific discovery.
  • Scientific progress depends on researchers asking new questions and finding ways to answer them.
  • OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that how more than 1,800 scientists used ChatGPT—and what they expect AI to mean for scientific discovery. Explore the findings in our fresh report.

Scientific progress depends on researchers asking new questions and finding ways to answer them. AI is becoming part of that work, but we’re still learning where it helps and what it could mean for discovery.

OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.

In a recent development, scientists used ChatGPT across the research process, from reviewing literature to analyzing evidence and developing ideas. Surveyed participants estimated that the same work, at the same quality, would have taken 1.9 times as long without AI. And 98% of those who answered our question about discovery timelines expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field.

By default, OpenAI does not use participants’ data from the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to train its models. To protect researchers’ privacy, we used tools called automated classifiers to sort messages by the type of research activity, such as reviewing literature, writing code, or analyzing data. The research team could see those categories, but did not read the underlying messages or ChatGPT’s responses.

We studied how scientists used ChatGPT across the research process.

#28636. The Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Its First Global South Language

📅 28 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2488 w)

The Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Its First Global South Language

📅 28 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English.
  • A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve.
  • According to recent reports, all of that makes one number (WER) harder to game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English.

Benchmarks decide what gets built. A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve. Much of the recent work on the leaderboard has gone into making the evaluation metrics more trustworthy:.

According to recent reports, all of that makes one number (WER) harder to game. It is still one number. A long line of work has shown that ASR error rates are not evenly distributed across the people using them. Racial disparities in automated speech recognition found commercial systems roughly twice as bad for Black speakers as for white speakers, and Quantifying Bias in Automatic Speech Recognition found further differences by gender, age and accent. None of that is visible on a leaderboard, and not because the leaderboard is hiding it. The test sets it runs on record what was mentioned and almost nothing about who said it.

To address this gap, we introduce two evaluation sets to the Open ASR Leaderboard: Monsoon en-IN and Monsoon hi-IN. Hindi, spoken by more than half a billion people, is the first Indic language on a multilingual tab that currently covers only European languages. Each set is released as a public split, available for self-scoring, and a private split withheld to limit benchmark-specific optimisation. The four splits are speaker-disjoint, comprising 4,888 speakers, with 12 speaker attributes recorded for each.

Sources indicate that A test set can only expose a failure mode it varies along. Most benchmarks are built from whatever audio was readily available. Monsoon was built to vary along nine axes: geography, age, gender, vocabulary, devices, acoustic environments, speech type, speech rate, and the existence of multiple valid transcripts for the same audio. Each is a way an aggregate WER can be right on average and wrong for a particular population.

The collection method follows from that.

Four splits, two languages, collected through one pipeline.

In a recent development, the data is sourced from unscripted dual-channel spontaneous conversations, with clips segmented from a single channel so that each clip carries one speaker. Along with the fields reported in the table, each clip also records occupation, education, marital status, income band, handset brand, current city and years in the current district.

Five clips from the public Indian English split, with the metadata each one carries:.

29-year-old woman, West Tripura, Tripura. Student, samsung SM-G781B.

It has been revealed that 32-year-old woman, Satna, Madhya Pradesh. Unemployed, samsung SM-E146B.

22-year-old man, Rohtas, Bihar. Student, motorola moto g54 5G.

Recent findings suggest that 27-year-old woman, Warangal, Telangana. Unemployed, vivo V2247.

Industry observers note that 57-year-old man, Puducherry. Private job, Xiaomi M2006C3LI.

Sources indicate that the English sets use standard string references, where the leaderboard's normaliser collapses most spelling variation. Hindi has far more of it, and no normaliser can resolve it, because the variants are not a fixed mapping between two conventions. The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, a list of the spellings that are accepted as correct.

In a recent development, monsoon is small measured in hours and large measured in speakers. That is the design, and it is where most of the value sits.

Speaker concentration and diversity beyond the fields above.

Three properties follow, and each is a claim about variance rather than volume.

According to recent reports, no voice carries the score: The ten largest contributors account for between 2.8% and 6.8% of total duration, and more than half of all speakers appear exactly once. A result on Monsoon is an average over hundreds of distinct voices, not a small number of talkers recorded at length. Test sets of comparable duration are usually constructed the other way.

Sources indicate that no region or handset carries it either: The Indian English public set draws on 428 native districts across 30 states and union territories; the Hindi sets, being a Hindi-belt language, concentrate more tightly but still span 202 and 295 districts. Recordings come from 315 to 582 distinct device models, with no single model exceeding 2.1% of segments in any subset. Corpora collected on standardised hardware overfit to one microphone response; this one cannot.

Indian English here is not one accent: This is English as it is spoken across the country, not the English of one region. All six zones are represented: in the public set, 35% of segments are contributed by southern speakers, 18% from the East, 18% from Central, 16% from the North and 11% from the West. The accent variation that follows from that spread is recorded in the metadata rather than asserted.

It has been revealed that monsoon ships 18 columns per segment, of which 12 are metadata, where most public ASR test sets ship an identifier, a transcript and a duration. Demographic fields are complete or near-complete; contributors consented to this use.

The two languages have different geographic shapes, and the shape is informative. The Hindi sets concentrate in the Hindi belt, with Uttar Pradesh accounting for roughly 40% of speakers, which is what a Hindi corpus sampled by population should look like. The Indian English sets are much flatter: no state exceeds 13%, and a third of speakers come from outside the eight largest. Public and private halves match closely on both.

In a recent development, indian state boundaries were drawn along linguistic lines, so district and state carry real accent signal, which is why these fields are released rather than summarised away. Analysis of this kind has been reported at scale for Indian ASR: district-level error rates spanning roughly 4% to 44%, with underrepresented regions well behind the Hindi belt and the metros, plus disaggregation by audio quality, speaking rate, utterance duration, gender, age and device. Those runs were on a closed benchmark. Monsoon makes the same class of analysis possible on a public leaderboard test set.

It has been revealed that broad geographic coverage requires recruitment across hundreds of districts rather than longer sessions from fewer speakers, and distributed recruitment at this scale introduces failure modes that a smaller collection does not face: contributors gaming the task, played-back audio submitted as live speech, and inattentive annotation. Each is addressed by an explicit check.

Sources indicate that recruitment and recording: Contributors were recruited through the Voice Arena community, a global digital platform whose reach extends into the rural and semi-urban districts that speech corpora rarely cover. Pairs then recorded two-person conversations over a peer-to-peer interface, dual-channel, on assigned everyday topics. Contributors used their own handsets and their own connections. Many of those are low-end devices on unstable bandwidth, which is why that condition is present in the released audio rather than filtered out of it. Prospective contributors completed a language proficiency screening before being granted recording access, were compensated, and provided informed consent covering use in training and distribution. A per-speaker duration cap, calibrated per language to the population size and geographic distribution of its speakers, prevented a small number of prolific contributors from dominating a language or region; more than half of the speakers in these sets contribute exactly one segment.

Sources indicate that elicitation: Eliciting spontaneous speech at scale presents its own difficulty, as contributors tend to produce short and sparse responses without structured guidance. Each conversation was therefore seeded with an open-ended narrative cue and progressively revealed follow-up questions, spanning domains including travel, healthcare, agriculture, education and digital services, guiding the exchange toward extended description without scripting it. Candidate topics were generated with large language models, then reviewed and localised by native-speaker linguists.

It has been revealed that quality control: Every recording passed a set of gating checks prior to transcription. The spoken language was verified against the assigned language using language identification models trained on human-annotated data across more than 30 languages. Speaker gender was confirmed against the self-reported label using a dedicated classifier, applied as corroboration of the self-report rather than as a replacement for it. A further model distinguished genuine spontaneous conversation from pre-recorded or played-back audio. Signal-to-noise ratio estimation removed recordings degraded beyond intelligibility, while natural environmental background noise was deliberately preserved so that the acoustic realism of in-the-wild speech is retained. Recordings clearing these checks were segmented by voice activity detection, split at two seconds of continuous silence or at a fifteen-second soft cap closed at the next detected silence. Segmentation was applied independently per channel, so every segment is single-speaker and single-channel. Segments then passed a DNSMOS P.808 check.

It has been revealed that transcription: Reference transcripts are human work. A first draft was generated by internal ASR models trained on in-domain data, none of which appear on any public leaderboard, so no system evaluated on these sets contributed to the references it is scored against. Every subsequent stage was performed by native-speaking linguists under a five-level protocol built on a strict separation of labour, in which each correction round is followed by an independent verification round performed by a different annotator, so no linguist audits their own output. A linguist first corrects the draft segment by segment against the acoustic signal; a second re-verifies it and flags residual disagreements. Subsequent levels iterate this cycle with fresh annotators, progressively resolving ambiguous phonetic realisations, code-switching boundaries, named entities, and orthographic consistency across spelling variants. Numerals are written as words, so that the transcript corresponds directly to what was spoken. Segments still flagged at the final level were returned for re-transcription before admission. Annotator behaviour was monitored automatically throughout, flagging submissions containing characters outside the target script, unnatural character or word repetitions, and unusually low or high edit counts.

In a recent development, what follows is one example, run on the public Indian English split, to show the kind of evaluation the metadata makes possible. It is not the finding the sets exist to deliver; it is an illustration of what becomes answerable once every clip carries a speaker.

Eight models on the leaderboard land between 4.81 and 4.99 WER on this set. That is 0.18 points from best to worst, inside what five hours can resolve. Ranked on the corpus, they are the same model.

According to recent reports, grouping speakers by region tells a different story. Each speaker's native district is rolled up to its zonal council, the Ministry of Home Affairs grouping of Indian states, giving five well-sampled zones. openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo varies by 0.46 points across them. mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507, fourteen hundredths of a point behind it on the corpus, varies by 1.68, running 4.38 in the Central zone against 6.06 in the East. Two systems that are indistinguishable on the leaderboard differ almost fourfold in how much their accuracy depends on where the speaker is from.

Recent findings suggest that which zone is hardest is not fixed either. ibm-granite/granite-speech-3.3-2b is worst in the North, microsoft/VibeVoice-ASR-HF in the South, mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 in the East. If a single region were simply harder to transcribe, every model would rank the zones the same way. They do not, which points at the models rather than the audio.

Region is one of twelve recorded attributes, and the zones above are a coarse rollup of 428 districts. The same breakdown runs on age, education, occupation and handset, and the released files carry everything needed to reproduce it. None of it is available for a test set that records only what was said.

English orthographic variation is bounded. British against American spelling, punctuation, casing, digits against words: a normaliser can map most of it to a single form, and the leaderboard's does. Hindi is not bounded in the same way. Everyday speech is heavily code-mixed, English-origin words have no settled Devanagari spelling, and compound forms are written joined or separated according to preference. A single phrase can have ten or more valid written forms, and no fixed mapping collapses them, because there is no canonical side to map to.

Scored with a single reference, WER rewards a system for producing the spelling the annotator happened to choose. Two systems that recognised the audio equally well can differ by several points on orthography alone.

Industry observers note that the Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, the set of written forms accepted as correct. Building it is manual work. Candidate variants are drawn from multiple ASR transcripts of the same audio and expanded with language models, then native-speaker linguists decide which are valid for that utterance and prune the rest, so only forms consistent with what was noted are admitted.

According to recent reports, thus, for Hindi we report the Orthographically-Informed Word Error Rate (OIWER), introduced by AI4Bharat, instead of WER. A hypothesis is aligned against the accepted set at each span, so any admitted form counts as correct and only genuine recognition errors are charged.

To quantify the effect, the same hypotheses were scored twice. Flattening each lattice to its first variant per span yields a single string reference of the kind a conventional benchmark provides; any of the admitted variants would serve equally well, and a different choice would yield a different reference. Scored against the flattened reference, error rates rise for every system, and they do not rise uniformly. Rankings change as a consequence. The figure below shows two pairs of systems that reverse order between the two references: under a single reference a system is rewarded in part for reproducing the annotator's orthography, whereas the lattice scores only recognition.

We also open source our implementation, voi-oiwer, so every result on these sets can be reproduced directly.

For the private splits, get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard and the Hugging Face team will run the evaluation. As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:.

Indian-English joins the main leaderboard as Voice Arena Monsoon, in the default column set rather than as an opt-in toggle, so it contributes to the headline Average WER for every model. The private split feeds the aggregated Private (conversational) column alongside Appen and DataoceanAI data. The public and private Hindi appears in the Multilingual tab, where a model is ranked only if it supports every selected language, making that column a like-for-like comparison. Alternative, select "Hindi" from the "Language dataset breakdown" dropdown menu.

Hindi is a sharp case of a general problem. Any language written more than one way, spoken by people a benchmark has not sampled, carries both of the failures described here. These sets do not fix them. What they add is a way to see them: a test set on a leaderboard the field already watches, carrying enough about each speaker and each reference that a difference between two systems can be traced to who was talking and how they write it, instead of disappearing into one number.

These four sets are part of Monsoon, Voice Arena's broader dataset initiative for the Global South.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we’re releasing a latest tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators.
  • Recent findings suggest that it is well⁠(opens in a fresh window) established⁠(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re releasing a latest tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on our Child Safety Blueprint and our ongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse. For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.

Recent findings suggest that it is well⁠(opens in a fresh window) established⁠(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.

Industry observers note that we’re building on our current protections with the release of a new image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.

Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)⁠(opens in a latest window), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.

We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.

It has been revealed that child safety is an industry-wide matter that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a upcoming window) and ROOST⁠(opens in a new window) to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window) CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program⁠(opens in a new window), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.

We’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.

It has been revealed that early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the new classifier with our current protections and found:.

The newly introduced classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag 48% fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.

Images flagged by the new classifier were about twice as likely to contain abuse.

Early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. In fal⁠(opens in a newly introduced window)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. invideo AI⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In SafetyKit⁠(opens in a new window)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected 90% of cases.

More information about the classifier is available in the CSAM classifier model card⁠(opens in a latest window). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through our intake form⁠. We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

In a recent development, we already prohibit CSAM, train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with upcoming product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.

It has been revealed that the warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

We developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including Protect Children⁠(opens in a new window), the Lucy Faithfull Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial⁠(opens in a new window) of deterrent messages.

The protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve published CSAM guidance⁠(opens in a new window) to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), NCMEC⁠(opens in a new window), and the Internet Watch Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.

The guidance provides clear rules, ways for owners to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our fresh image classifier, Moderation API⁠(opens in a new window), ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop⁠(opens in a new window), and dedicated CSAM detection services such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window).

Our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission newly introduced guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.

We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.

It has been revealed that protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’ve discussed publicly with Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.

We’re also supporting child-safety law enforcement units with fresh tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.

According to recent reports, the initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences.

These efforts share one goal: preventing harm to children and strengthening the response when abuse occurs. We’ll continue improving our safeguards while empowering child protection organizations, developers, researchers, and investigators with the tools, resources, and expertise they need to protect children, combat exploitation, and bring perpetrators to justice. By working together, we can harness the power of AI to make a meaningful difference in the fight against child sexual exploitation and abuse.

#28634. Introducing @huggingface/kernels: 200+ WebGPU Kernels for Local AI

📅 01 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1577 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing @huggingface/kernels: 200+ WebGPU Kernels for Local AI

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible.
  • Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.
  • In a recent development, the collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible. Getting there is a multi-layer effort: models need browser-friendly representations, runtimes need to build efficient execution intends, and the individual GPU operations at the bottom of the stack need to make the most of many different devices and browser implementations.

Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.

In a recent development, the collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads. More importantly, each kernel is published as a complete, versioned package: its interface, shader templates, correctness cases, benchmark cases, and usage instructions all live together on the Hub.

Sources indicate that we are also launching Fleet, an in-browser GPU benchmarking and testing suite that runs and scores the kernels on your hardware. Beyond the results for your own machine, Fleet gives the community a way to contribute performance and correctness evidence from devices we could never cover in a conventional test lab. With your consent, every run adds private evidence that can help us find failures (incorrect results, pathologically slow cases, etc.), improve kernel variants, and make better optimization decisions across real-world hardware.

A model running in the browser eventually becomes a sequence of GPU operations: matrix multiplications, normalizations, convolutions, attention primitives, quantization operations, data-layout transformations, and many more. WebGPU makes these operations available across modern browsers through a portable API, while WGSL provides a common language for the shaders that execute them.

Portability, however, does not automatically mean performance. Two shaders can implement the same operation and produce the same output while behaving completely differently across different accelerators. Workgroup sizes, memory access patterns, vectorization, data types, and fusion strategies can all affect performance. The best choice can also change with the input shape, device, browser, and available WebGPU features.

This is why kernels form a foundational layer of fast browser inference. Higher-level runtimes can only be as efficient as the operations they dispatch. By making those operations individually discoverable, testable, benchmarkable, and versioned, we can improve the foundation independently while keeping a stable contract for the layers above it.

Each kernel in the collection has its own repository and kernel card. The card documents the operation's semantics, inputs, outputs, attributes, supported data types, source files, and a ready-to-run @huggingface/kernels example.

In a recent development, for example, ai.onnx.Add implements elementwise addition with multidirectional broadcasting. It is one of the simplest operations in a neural network, used everywhere from residual connections to adding a bias. Its card documents the two inputs, the broadcasted output shape, supported data types, and the variants available for different shapes and devices.

Behind the card, the repository contains the artifacts needed to understand and evaluate the implementation:.

This structure turns a shader into a reusable software artifact. The interface is inspectable without reading WGSL, correctness and performance cases travel with the implementation, and published versions can be loaded explicitly rather than depending on an unversioned file URL. Our kernels can also serve as reference implementations for developers building custom WebGPU kernels or integrating these operations into their own runtimes.

Running these kernels requires a browser with WebGPU support. WebGPU availability depends on the browser, operating system, GPU, and driver. You can check for it in JavaScript with "gpu" in navigator.

@huggingface/kernels provides the bridge between a kernel repository and your application. Call getKernel with a Hub repository ID and a contract version, then invoke the returned function with typed input data and tensor shapes. Here is a small bias-add example:.

Sources indicate that the second input is broadcast across the first dimension, producing an output with shape [2, 3]. The loader derives that output shape and logical data type from the manifest contract and the inputs, then allocates c automatically.

Addition on six floats is deliberately the smallest possible demo. At this size, the GPU round trip costs far more than the math. The point is the call pattern: it stays exactly the same for the heavyweight operations where optimized kernels actually pay off, such as matrix multiplication (ai.onnx.MatMul). Only the repository ID and the inputs change.

Sources indicate that even this elementary operation illustrates why kernels need variants. Equal-shape addition can use a direct vectorized path, while broadcasted inputs need different indexing logic. The published Add kernel includes variants for equal shapes, vectorized broadcasting, scalar processing, and general broadcasting. The runtime can select an implementation that fits the current call and device without changing the application-facing API.

In a recent development, the version: 1 option selects version 1 of the published kernel contract. It is separate from an ONNX opset, an operator's since_version, or a model revision. Keeping those concepts separate lets applications depend on a stable JavaScript-facing contract while kernel implementations evolve behind it.

So, how much of a difference do optimized kernels actually make? We put our collection head-to-head with ORT WebGPU on an Apple M4 GPU, using ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0-dev.20260826-b1f76d586a. We started with 1,756 test cases across all 207 operations and kept the 809 cases where both sides produced matching outputs and reliable timings.

According to recent reports, across those comparisons, our kernels were 2.57x faster by geometric mean and 1.90x faster at the median, with 629 wins, 176 losses, and 4 ties. Here is a closer look at four familiar operations:.

Some individual wins were much bigger. A particularly difficult bilinear Einsum case (i,ij,j with size 4096) ran in 0.136 ms with our kernel versus 1,396 ms with ORT WebGPU: more than 10,000x faster. A row-wise CumSum over [256, 4096] was 301x faster, at 0.016 ms versus 4.784 ms. These are unusual cases rather than the speedups you should expect everywhere, but they show how much a specialized kernel can help when a general implementation hits a slow path.

We timed the work done on the GPU itself, leaving out setup such as loading kernels, creating sessions, uploading inputs, compiling shaders, and reading outputs back. Very short workloads are naturally harder to measure, and small cases can benefit from the GPU cache, so these numbers are best read as a useful comparison rather than a promise for every application.

They are also results for individual operations, not complete models. Exact performance will change across GPUs and browsers, which is why Fleet is so important for building a broader picture.

We are also working with the ONNX Runtime team to upstream these improvements so they can benefit the broader ONNX Runtime Web ecosystem.

Sources indicate that webGPU performance varies across GPUs, browsers, and drivers, so results from one machine only tell part of the story. Fleet lets anyone run correctness and performance checks in the browser and see how the kernels behave on their hardware.

In a recent development, with consent, each run privately contributes evidence that helps us spot device-specific failures, compare variants, and improve selection rules. The goal is simple: use broad, real-world coverage to make the kernels faster and more reliable for everyone.

The initial 207 kernels are a starting point, not the end state. Publishing kernels independently on the Hub gives us a common place to inspect contracts, compare implementations, reproduce correctness checks, and improve performance without embedding every shader directly into every runtime.

The collection is also part of the Hub's broader kernel ecosystem: on the Kernels page, the WebGPU kernels sit alongside kernels for CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and other platforms, and can be filtered, sorted, and explored like any other artifact on the Hub.

The pieces reinforce one another:.

Sources indicate that this is the low-level foundation for the next steps in our browser inference stack. We are excited to connect these kernels to higher-level model tooling, continue expanding operation coverage, and make fast local inference easier to use across the WebAI ecosystem.

Explore the WebGPU kernel collection, try @huggingface/kernels, and join the Fleet to contribute evidence from your device and help us make the kernels better for everyone.

The Fleet part may matter as much as the kernels. The 809 comparable cases on an M4 are useful, but browser, driver and device variance is where WebGPU tends to get painful. Will Fleet eventually expose per-device distributions, or is the plan to use the runs only for aggregate selection rules?

In an automated build system, I could see per device kernels, made more interesting by fusion of ops.

The area that obviously needs more attention are the 947 tests that did not result in reliable output. This could be the test, it could be that the ORT WebGPU is wrong, or the upcoming kernel is wrong, or the test harness had complications, hard to know from the outside. Perhaps the Fleet thing is meant to improve this.

Very excited to see such attention at making WebGPU first class in ML!

@sroussey Agreed—the excluded 947 need a taxonomy before the 2.57× summary can travel. I'd want counts by operation and device for unsupported, ORT mismatch, new-kernel mismatch, and harness/timeout, with raw failing cases downloadable. Then Fleet can optimize only within a proven-correct compatibility envelope; fusion and per-device tuning become much safer.

Industry observers note that excellent! This will help our WebAI community continue developing highly optimized solutions. Many thanks @Xenova and @nico-martin for the great work you have been doing.

BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.
  • Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a latest method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.
  • In a recent development, A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.

Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a latest method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.

In a recent development, A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following. But the individual tasks inside it may depend on more than that stated goal. Take BBQ, a benchmark designed to test whether models rely on social stereotypes. One question asks about a grandson and grandfather trying to book an Uber. It probes age bias, but also requires the model to track who’s who and reason from the evidence provided rather than assumptions.

And even within a single benchmark, different groups of questions and tasks can measure different things. WildJailbreak, for example, includes harmful jailbreak prompts alongside benign prompts designed to test whether a model refuses harmless requests too often. The harmful prompts are more closely associated with safety, while the benign prompts are more closely associated with general reasoning. Averaging them into a single benchmark score can obscure that difference.

Sources indicate that benchMIRT helps researchers separate those signals and see what’s actually driving a benchmark’s score. It does this by analyzing how models perform on each question or task and estimating which underlying capabilities are most closely associated with getting it right.

BenchMIRT takes cues from Item Response Theory (IRT), a technique originating in psychometrics—the field concerned with measuring abilities and traits from patterns of test responses. IRT starts from a simple idea: not every question tells you the same amount about the person taking a test. Some are harder than others, and some do a better job of distinguishing stronger performers from weaker ones.

Recent findings suggest that researchers have previously applied single-dimensional IRT to individual benchmarks, including in our Fluid Benchmarking work. BenchMIRT extends that approach with multidimensional IRT, or MIRT, allowing it to separate multiple capabilities that may contribute to performance on the same questions.

Sources indicate that benchMIRT applies IRT at both the model and question level. For a given model, it estimates the model’s strength on the capabilities reflected across the selected benchmarks. For each question, it estimates how difficult the question is and how well it distinguishes models that are stronger or weaker on those capabilities.

Sources indicate that we trained BenchMIRT on benchmarking results from 100 LLMs across 16 benchmarks and more than 34K questions. Six of those benchmarks measure general reasoning, including MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MATH, and BBH. The other 10 come from our Olmo 3 safety suite, including HarmBench, StrongReject, WildJailbreak, BBQ, WMDP, and XSTest.

Sources indicate that crucially, we didn’t tell BenchMIRT which benchmarks were measuring which capabilities. It independently recovered two dominant dimensions: safety and general reasoning. When we repeated our analysis from scratch, those same two dimensions emerged each time, suggesting the result was stable rather than specific to one analysis.

For many benchmarks, BenchMIRT largely confirmed their intended focus: strong performance on reasoning benchmarks tracked with reasoning ability, while strong performance on jailbreak and harmful-content benchmarks tracked with safety.

But BenchMIRT also revealed a more complicated picture in some evaluations.

Sources indicate that BBQ, which evaluates social bias and is commonly grouped with safety benchmarks, aligned much more strongly with general reasoning in BenchMIRT’s analysis. That means a low BBQ score may partly reflect difficulty understanding or reasoning through certain questions, rather than safety behavior alone.

According to recent reports, WMDP behaves differently from most safety benchmarks. It tests dangerous dual-use knowledge in areas such as biology, chemistry, and cybersecurity—for example, knowledge that could help someone misuse a biological agent or exploit a computer system. BenchMIRT found that WMDP scores were more strongly associated with general reasoning than with safety. Stronger general reasoning, however, was associated with lower WMDP scores, because the benchmark counts refusing or failing to provide the dangerous knowledge as the desired response.

Industry observers note that these findings don’t necessarily mean the benchmarks are flawed or incomplete. Rather, they show that a single benchmark score can combine several different signals—and that BenchMIRT can help disentangle those signals and make the score easier to interpret.

According to recent reports, item difficulty and discrimination in both dimensions for Harmbench. Dimension 0 models the safety dimension, while Dimension 1 maps to the general reasoning dimension.

Bar size and direction show the Pearson correlation, across 100 open-weight LLMs, between BenchMIRT ability scores and benchmark scores on a −1 to 1 scale—pink for general reasoning and teal for safety; bars extending left of center are negative. Bold with underline marks each row’s stronger correlation, except where the two are too close to separate; asterisks mark p < 0.01.

BenchMIRT can also help identify which questions in an evaluation are most informative about the capability the benchmark is trying to measure.

Using BenchMIRT’s question-level estimates, we ranked questions across the same 16 benchmarks used to train BenchMIRT and kept those that did the best job of distinguishing stronger from weaker models, while still preserving a mix of easier and harder questions.

Across those benchmarks, keeping only 10% of the questions generally preserved nearly the same picture of which models were stronger or weaker on the underlying safety or reasoning capability as using the full set. Keeping 50% of the questions often matched the full benchmark’s measure of those capabilities even more closely.

BenchMIRT can also use the patterns it learns across models and questions to predict how a model would perform on a benchmark question it hasn’t been observed answering. In our experiments, it correctly predicted whether a model would answer a held-out question correctly 79% of the time. By comparison, a simpler approach that assumes a model will perform on each question about as well as it does on the benchmark overall was correct 70% of the time.

In practice, that means BenchMIRT can estimate model performance more precisely from what it has already learned about the model’s abilities and the demands of each question, without needing to evaluate every model on every question.

Recent findings suggest that benchMIRT offers a way to better understand and refine the benchmarks researchers use to evaluate model capabilities. By looking at individual questions rather than only overall scores, it can reveal when a benchmark mixes together different capabilities, identify clusters of questions that behave differently from the rest, and surface questions that add little useful information about the capability the benchmark is meant to measure.

There are key limitations. The models we used to train and evaluate BenchMIRT were all released by March 2025, so our analysis doesn’t capture how BenchMIRT behaves on newer generations of LLMs. And the dimensions BenchMIRT discovers depend on the benchmark set it’s given—safety and reasoning emerged as the dominant dimensions across the 16 benchmarks we selected for this project, but a different mix of evaluations could surface different underlying capabilities.

There are trade-offs, too. If the goal is to rank models by their predicted performance on randomly held-out items, the benchmark’s average score performs slightly better than BenchMIRT. BenchMIRT’s advantage is the finer-grained picture it provides of performance on individual questions.

That question-level detail can also cut both ways: the same estimates that help identify a benchmark’s most informative safety questions could be used to remove them, producing a weaker evaluation that an unsafe model could pass. Existing tools already make it possible to trim evaluations in similar ways, and we think the added transparency into what benchmark questions are actually measuring is worth that risk—but it’s a real one.

Still, we see BenchMIRT – and future tools like it – as a step toward more targeted benchmark design and efficient evaluation. By showing which questions are actually driving a benchmark’s results, these approaches could help researchers build evaluations that are smaller, more focused, and easier to interpret, while giving a clearer picture of the capabilities they’re meant to measure.

In a recent development, good read! Reliable evaluation is essential for understanding how well AI systems perform and where they need improvement. Benchmarking and systematic testing can help developers make better decisions about model selection, application quality, and readiness for real-world use. In Generative AI app development, these practices are particularly useful for identifying limitations before expanding access or introducing additional features. This guide offers related insights into taking Claude AI applications from MVP to scale: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-development/claude-ai-app-development-mvp-to-scale.

Today we’re launching OpenAI for Chile, a partnership with the Government of Chile, led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, to support responsible AI adoption in public administration, build civil servants’ skills and help local startups develop useful AI applications.

The partnership builds on Chile’s National AI Policy and action blueprint⁠(opens in a fresh window), which support talent development, research and responsible adoption.

The Memorandum of Understanding was signed on the sidelines of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California, with Minister Ximena Lincolao leading the agreement on behalf of Chile.

Recent findings suggest that the partnership is supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s American SI Exports Program⁠(opens in a fresh window), of which OpenAI is an anchor partner, helping Chile advance its own AI ambitions through public sector innovation, skills development, and entrepreneurship.

The partnership will explore technology adoption in the ministry’s administrative processes, including potential support from OpenAI on adopting newly introduced models, alongside advice and training for ministry personnel.

For civil servants, the partnership will explore practical AI literacy, upskilling and reskilling tailored to their roles. Activities could include workshops and a train-the-trainer approach, covering effective use of AI tools, checking outputs, protecting sensitive information and maintaining human oversight.

To support Chile’s AI startup and innovation ecosystem, the partners will explore access to relevant OpenAI programs and technology, practical learning, technical guidance and mentorship. Cooperation could also connect entrepreneurs with public institutions, universities and other local partners to develop applications that support Chile’s economic development and public-service priorities.

A joint task force of ministry and OpenAI representatives is expected to agree priorities and an initial workplan, with leads, milestones and measures of success for each activity.

It has been revealed that specific activities, eligibility, resources and access to technology will be agreed separately. The MoU sets no investment or purchasing commitment. Activities will be subject to appropriate safeguards for privacy, information security and responsible use.

Industry observers note that openAI for Chile is part of OpenAI for Countries, our global initiative to help countries use AI to advance their national priorities, strengthen their economies and expand opportunity. We work with governments and local partners to turn AI’s potential into practical benefits for their people.

#28630. Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3949 w)
