Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.
  • In a recent development, that is embarrassing onstage.
  • Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

In a recent development, that is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

It has been revealed that in an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a new guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

According to recent reports, standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

It has been revealed that ⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

Sources indicate that this isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

This is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a new source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

It has been revealed that 2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":.

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Recent findings suggest that nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

Sources indicate that the consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

Recent findings suggest that the middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

In a recent development, mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

According to recent reports, the sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

It has been revealed that if accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”.

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

What I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

According to recent reports, reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

It has been revealed that thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

On your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:.

Recent findings suggest that I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each latest task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • How Codex runs commands on your machine with limits you control.
  • Sources indicate that at OpenAI, we take a defense in depth⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) approach when it comes to safeguarding agents.
  • According to recent reports, A ⁠(opens in a new window)sandbox⁠(opens in a new window) limits what a program can access while it runs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How Codex runs commands on your machine with limits you control.

By Michael Bolin, Member of Technical Staff.

Sources indicate that at OpenAI, we take a defense in depth⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) approach when it comes to safeguarding agents. While our investments in training and alignment are fundamental to this effort, we also implement features in our agentic harness, Codex⁠(opens in a new window), to provide additional protections. Because one of the most common (and potentially risky) things Codex does is run commands on your computer, we built the Codex sandbox so Codex can work in your existing environment within filesystem and network limits you control.

According to recent reports, A ⁠(opens in a new window)sandbox⁠(opens in a new window) limits what a program can access while it runs. For a photo-organizing task, you might configure the Codex sandbox to let commands read and modify files in ~/Pictures while blocking network access to prevent uploads. For code review, you might allow access to online documentation while keeping source files read-only. Users configure the Codex sandbox through ⁠(opens in a new window)permission profiles⁠(opens in a new window), which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session.

In a recent development, in this article, we’ll start with the tradeoffs behind Codex’s sandbox defaults, then explain the sandbox’s design and how the harness uses it to run commands. We’ll show how end users and enterprises can tailor its permissions to their needs and how developers can reuse the sandbox in their own tools. Finally, we’ll examine how these restrictions are enforced on macOS, Linux, and Windows.

In Codex, our philosophy is to specify conservative defaults for the sandbox that still enable meaningful work. For example, with a Git repository as the workspace root, the built-in :workspace permission profile:.

Allows writes within the workspace, while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only. This lets Codex edit source code without seeking permission for every change, while preventing direct changes to .codex/config.toml or Git hooks under .git/hooks.

Allows broad filesystem reads, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions. Compilers, runtimes, and build tools depend on SDKs, libraries, and configuration outside the repository. Restricting reads to the workspace would break many ordinary workflows. The tradeoff is that sensitive files elsewhere on the machine may also remain readable (such as config files containing API keys).

Sources indicate that disables network access. This blocks direct uploads to external services, including attempts to exfiltrate data the command can read. It also prevents legitimate operations such as downloading dependencies, which require additional access.

Recent findings suggest that these restrictions prevent a large class of bad behavior, but harmful actions are still possible. For example, the agent could inject malicious code into a locally installed package such as node_modules/prettier. Such a change might not appear in git status because node_modules is often ignored by Git. If the user’s editor runs that copy of Prettier on save, simply saving a file could execute the malicious code outside the Codex sandbox. This is why we take a defense in depth approach: the sandbox limits what commands can access, while training and alignment help the model use that access in accordance with the user’s intent.

For guidance on tailoring sandbox permissions and combining them with other protections in an enterprise environment, see the Codex security cookbook⁠(opens in a latest window).

According to recent reports, virtual machines and containers⁠(opens in a latest window) are two popular mechanisms used for sandboxing, but we take a different approach with the Codex sandbox. Instead of moving computation to a separate environment to provide isolation, Codex uses each platform’s sandboxing facilities to constrain commands running in the user’s existing environment.For many developers, their laptop serves as a bespoke dev environment that they can change on a whim. Reproducing that environment in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host.

Recent findings suggest that for example, consider using Codex to develop an iOS app on a Mac. If you decided to sandbox Codex by running it inside Docker, Codex would not be able to run the iOS build toolchain composed of native Mac executables, nor could it launch the iPhone simulator to run the code. A Docker-based workflow could delegate builds and simulator operations to the Mac host, but those operations would execute outside the container’s sandbox and would need their own restrictions. For Codex, we prefer to keep things simple by investing heavily in OS-specific sandboxing so Codex can run in the environment that is most appropriate to the task at hand.

According to recent reports, the harness exposes these OS-specific sandboxing mechanisms through a common API across macOS, Windows, and Linux. This API takes a command and a permission profile. If the permission profile allows limited network access, the caller must supply a network proxy to enforce those limits:.

This function starts the process in a sandbox and returns a Child handle the harness can use to wait for it to finish. Each child process inherits its parent’s sandbox constraints, so those restrictions apply throughout the process tree initiated by the command, even to descendants that outlive the original process.

The following diagram indicates how these pieces fit together, from configuration to running a sandboxed command. The sections that follow explain each stage.

Industry observers note that as explained in Unrolling the Codex Agent Loop, the Codex harness is responsible for executing tool calls generated by the model. For coding tasks, the most commonly used tool is a shell tool, which runs commands much as a user would in an interactive shell such as Bash. Here we’ll examine the one-shot ⁠(opens in a new window)exec_command⁠(opens in a new window) shell tool⁠(opens in a new window) to illustrate how the harness employs the sandbox to achieve the desired protections.This is a simplified version of how the exec_command tool call would be honored by the Codex harness without sandboxing:.

Sources indicate that to sandbox the command, the harness replaces the call to subprocess.Popen() with spawn_command_under_sandbox(). The harness supplies the permission profile and, when needed, the network proxy:.

The exec_command tool also lets the model request different permissions for an individual command, but the harness decides whether to grant the request:.

When use_default is specified, the harness uses the default sandbox config for the turn. with_additional_permissions requests expanded access within the sandbox, while require_escalated requests execution outside it. The harness evaluates the request based on the user’s preferences before executing the command. (For example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a upcoming window).) If execution is authorized, Codex will pass the appropriate permission_profile and network_proxy to perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing() with the command arguments from the original ExecCommandToolCall.

The shell tool is the primary consumer of spawn_command_under_sandbox(), and the harness also reuses its sandboxing infrastructure for operations such as reading and modifying local files. This reuse extends beyond the harness: the codex sandbox command lets you incorporate sandboxed command execution into your own tools, as we’ll see later. Next, we’ll look at how permission profiles are defined.

A named permission profile lets you reuse the same filesystem and network restrictions across projects. You can define your own profiles under [permissions] in config.toml. For example, the following defines a profile named dev that extends⁠(opens in a new window) the built-in :workspace profile:.

In a recent development, the dev profile adds write access to ~/build-cache and places additional restrictions on files in the workspace. Filesystem entries can grant read-only access (read), grant read and write access (write), or block access entirely (deny).

According to recent reports, the :workspace_roots table lets you define rules for paths relative to a project’s workspace roots. By default, the Codex CLI uses its working directory as its sole workspace root, while the ChatGPT desktop app uses the project’s source folders. Codex applies each rule to every root, so the .vscode entry in dev makes the .vscode directory read-only under each root.

In addition to its own rules, dev inherits the following protections from :workspace:.

When it comes to configuring the network for the sandbox in Codex, there are roughly three options:.

Disable all network access (default for the :workspace profile).

Enable full, direct network access (default for the :danger-full-access profile).

Restrict network access to a proxy, which decides what to let through based on the permission profile.

To give dev direct network access, set permissions.dev.network.enabled = true at the top level of config.toml. This grants full network access when the network proxy is disabled.

To restrict dev to a set of domains, enable the network proxy and configure its domain rules:.

According to recent reports, domain rules support exact names and wildcard patterns, with explicit deny rules taking precedence over allow rules. Requests to other domains require approval or are blocked, as described in Network proxy below.

Individual people can configure defaults that apply across projects and override them for a particular trusted project. Enterprise administrators may also want to configure defaults for their users and constrain which settings those users can change. Codex supports both through layered configuration and managed requirements.

In a recent development, as described in Configuration precedence,⁠(opens in a upcoming window) Codex merges settings from multiple config.toml files. Tables are merged recursively, with the higher-precedence source winning when values conflict. Arrays are replaced as a whole.

Recent findings suggest that this is why permission profiles use tables for filesystem paths and network domains. A team can add or override individual entries in its own configuration and automatically inherit changes to all other entries in the organization’s base configuration:.

Administrators can also supply managed requirements⁠(opens in a latest window) through requirements.toml to constrain users’ configuration choices. These requirements can come from multiple sources, including system files and cloud-provided policy. A common use case is to specify allowed_permission_profiles to constrain the set of permission profiles an enterprise user can select. For example, an administrator could specify these cloud requirements:.

The cloud requirements would take precedence over the system requirements file at /etc/codex/requirements.toml, so an entry in that file cannot override the explicit ":danger-full-access" = false above. Leaving :workspace unspecified allows another requirements layer to supply that entry. Profiles whose entries are false or absent from the final merged table are unavailable.This separation lets organizations enforce limits while owners tailor their configuration within those limits. The resulting permission profiles can be used by the harness or applied directly to a command, as we’ll see next.

Recent findings suggest that the Codex CLI provides a sandbox command to facilitate running an arbitrary command under a permission profile defined in the Codex config. This is commonly used to test out the profile, ensuring that the sandbox prevents the behavior it was designed to block.

Industry observers note that for example, the following command attempts to configure VS Code to run a malicious auto-formatter on save. Assuming .vscode already exists, the dev profile defined above should block this write because that directory is read-only (codex sandbox treats cwd as a workspace root by default):.

Indeed, on macOS this fails with:.

Recent findings suggest that the codex sandbox command makes Codex’s sandboxing mechanism available independently of an agent session. You can use the same configuration language and platform-specific enforcement to constrain commands launched by your own tools.

In a recent development, for a stdio MCP server configured in config.toml, the Codex harness does not attempt to sandbox the command used to start the server. Codex cannot reliably infer which files or network services that server needs, so applying a default sandbox profile could break an otherwise valid configuration.

For example, the standard way to configure the @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory⁠(opens in a new window) MCP server for use with Codex is as follows:.

Industry observers note that because this npx command runs unsandboxed, it can write files and make network requests with the same permissions as the user running Codex, which is overly permissive. To lock it down, we can define a permission profile named memory-mcp and then wrap the original npx command with codex sandbox --permission-profile memory-mcp to limit where the server can write and to prevent it from accessing the network:.

Before starting the server, create its data directory and populate the npm cache with the pinned package. That lets npx --offline launch the server under a profile that disables network access:.

Once the package is cached, Codex can start the memory server without network access, with writes limited to the npm cache and the server’s data directory.

Industry observers note that the sandbox implementation turns a permission profile into restrictions enforced by the operating system. The network proxy’s core request-handling and policy logic is shared across all three major operating systems, while proxy setup and integration with the sandbox are OS-specific. We’ll examine the shared proxy first, followed by the implementations for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

To enforce a permission profile’s network restrictions, the harness starts a network proxy and configures the sandbox to allow connections to it while blocking direct connections to external hosts. The proxy checks each request against the profile’s domain rules to determine whether to forward it.

In a recent development, in the Codex repo, the network proxy is implemented in the codex-network-proxy⁠(opens in a fresh window) crate, which the harness uses as a library, though it can also be built as a standalone CLI⁠(opens in a new window). When enabled, codex-network-proxy starts both an HTTP proxy and a SOCKS5 proxy by default. These proxy addresses are communicated to the process spawned by the sandbox via environment variables. In addition to injecting standard environment variables such as HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, and ALL_PROXY, a number of well-known application-specific environment variables⁠(opens in a new window) (such as PIP_PROXY) are injected, as well. Admittedly, not all programs honor these environment variables. If a program attempts a direct connection to an external host, the operating system’s sandbox restrictions block it, as described in the platform-specific sections below.

The network proxy is responsible for implementing the network restrictions defined in a permission profile. For example, the dev profile shown earlier allows requests to *.openai.com and explicitly denies requests to evil.example. When a request targets a domain that does not match an allow or deny rule, the proxy can suspend the request while it delegates to the harness for approval. Like the shell command example, Codex may prompt the user directly, or it might route the request to auto-review⁠(opens in a new window). Upon receiving a decision, the proxy either allows the request to proceed or rejects it with an error response.

In a recent development, the order matters here because even a DNS lookup can leak information encoded in a hostname. The proxy therefore resolves the requested hostname only after determining that it is allowed or approved. Note that broad wildcard rules or access to DNS services can still permit DNS-based exfiltration.

Sources indicate that on macOS, Codex uses Seatbelt⁠(opens in a upcoming window), Apple’s kernel-enforced sandboxing mechanism. Seatbelt policies are written in Sandbox Profile Language (SBPL), a Scheme-based language for expressing sandbox restrictions. Codex invokes Seatbelt through macOS’s /usr/bin/sandbox-exec command. Like codex sandbox, it takes options describing the sandbox followed by the command to run:.

According to recent reports, the PROFILE is a string of SBPL that contains entries that configure the sandbox. For example, the following SBPL snippet makes /dev/null and /dev/zero readable and writable under the sandbox policy:.

When the network proxy is enabled as part of a sandbox invocation, rules like the following are injected into the profile to limit connections to the appropriate local ports:.

Codex’s base profile starts with (deny default), so outbound connections remain blocked unless explicitly allowed.

Finally, the SBPL can contain placeholders using (param):.

which are populated by the -Dkey=value options passed to sandbox-exec.

Recent findings suggest that to implement its own sandbox API, Codex builds up the list of arguments⁠(opens in a latest window) to sandbox-exec starting from a base policy⁠(opens in a new window), and then uses permission_profile and other context to amend it to produce the complete Seatbelt profile. The resulting profile and accompanying -D arguments configure the restrictions enforced by Seatbelt, while the network proxy enforces additional network rules. With the full arg list assembled, the invocation of sandbox-exec is straightforward.

Generating the correct SBPL is challenging because Apple does not document the language for third-party use. Indeed, man sandbox-exec states The sandbox-exec command is DEPRECATED (as is the sandbox_init() library function documented via man 3 sandbox_init). Despite the deprecation warning, macOS still ships Seatbelt profiles in /usr/share/sandbox, and third-party software, including Google Chrome and Chromium⁠(opens in a latest window), continues to rely on Seatbelt. As such, we plan to continue to use Seatbelt for the foreseeable future.

To create the sandbox on Linux, Codex uses a combination of bubblewrap⁠(opens in a latest window) (bwrap), a command-line tool for constructing isolated environments, and seccomp-bpf⁠(opens in a new window), a Linux kernel mechanism for filtering system calls. An internal helper named codex-linux-sandbox coordinates the setup. Like sandbox-exec on macOS, it takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run:.

Sources indicate that when filesystem isolation or proxy routing is required, codex-linux-sandbox invokes bwrap to create the initial sandbox environment. bwrap then releases codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec inside it. This second invocation uses seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions before running the user’s command.

To construct that initial sandbox environment, Codex uses bubblewrap to create a filesystem view in a separate mount namespace that reflects the permission profile’s filesystem rules. Because this is fundamental to the sandbox implementation, Codex vendors its own copy of bwrap in case the user has not installed their own, but it prefers a compatible installation of ⁠(opens in a upcoming window)bwrap⁠(opens in a new window) found on PATH, when available. Empirically, some Linux distributions disable access to user namespaces by default⁠(opens in a new window), but grant an exception for the system bwrap.

Also like sandbox-exec, bwrap takes a sandbox configuration followed by a command to run within the sandbox. Instead of using a custom config language like SBPL, bwrap uses individual flags for configuration. Codex uses the following options to create the filesystem view:.

--bind to specify a writable file or directory.

--ro-bind to specify a read-only file or directory.

--perms 000 --tmpfs DIR --remount-ro DIR to deny access to DIR.

--perms 000 --ro-bind-data FD FILE to deny access to FILE (where FD is an open file descriptor to /dev/null).

To apply deny globs using these options, Codex expands them to concrete paths before launching each command. Fresh matching paths are not automatically added to that command’s sandbox restrictions.

Codex also specifies options such as --unshare-ipc and --unshare-pid to prevent the sandbox from accessing other types of resources on the host, so bubblewrap affects more than just file visibility.

Industry observers note that when using bubblewrap, Codex passes --unshare-net whenever networking is disabled or connections must go through the network proxy, which will create a upcoming network namespace for the sandbox. We then use seccomp-bpf to apply additional restrictions on the networking system calls and socket families available to the command.

Industry observers note that specifically, we use the seccompiler crate⁠(opens in a latest window) to dynamically compile a BPF program based on the desired filters⁠(opens in a new window) and apply it to a launcher process in the sandbox so the constraints are inherited by the entire process tree. As such, bwrap does not run the user’s command, but runs the codex-linux-sandbox launcher with its own config args followed by the user’s command:.

To apply seccomp filters without elevated privileges, the launcher sets Linux’s no_new_privs flag⁠(opens in a new window). This flag is inherited by child processes and prevents them from gaining additional privileges when executing another program, such as a setuid executable.

The seccomp filters depend on the network configuration. When network access is disabled, we block a number of network-related syscalls, such as connect(2) and bind(2). Though when the network proxy is enabled in the sandbox, we allow IP sockets so the TCP listener created by codex-linux-sandbox can be reached, but block the creation of standalone Unix domain sockets by default, as those could enable inadvertent access to resources from the host.

It has been revealed that when the sandbox configuration merits the use of the network proxy, the Codex harness creates one instance of the proxy that can be reused across multiple invocations of codex-linux-sandbox within the same Codex thread. Each sandbox needs a way to reach that shared proxy from its isolated network namespace. Codex provides a loopback TCP listener inside that namespace and arranges for a process outside the sandbox to accept its connections and relay them to the proxy.

Sources indicate that the following diagrams illustrate this setup for one proxy endpoint, with one connection through it shown in the final diagram. Before launching bubblewrap, codex-linux-sandbox creates a Unix socket pair to serve as a control channel and forks itself. The child runs run_host_bridge() and waits to receive the listener’s file descriptor over that channel:.

In this example, the parent process uses exec to replace its program image with bwrap. This sets up the sandbox and rolls out codex-linux-sandbox --apply-seccomp-then-exec within it, passing along the FD for the control channel:.

Inside the sandbox’s network namespace, the second invocation of codex-linux-sandbox creates a loopback TCP listener and passes its file descriptor via the socket. The listener remains associated with the sandbox’s network namespace, allowing the child process that remained outside the sandbox to accept connections from sandboxed programs while opening its upstream connections in the host’s network namespace. After the handoff, both processes close their control-channel descriptors, and the process inside the sandbox closes its copy of the listener.

Recent findings suggest that once the TCP listener is ready, the process inside the sandbox sets the appropriate value for HTTP_PROXY⁠(opens in a fresh window) and related environment variables to point to that listener. It then applies seccomp before forking and executing the user’s command:.

According to recent reports, the process outside the sandbox keeps the listener open. For each accepted connection, it opens a connection to the configured proxy and relays data in both directions.This additional machinery gives the command its own network namespace, including a separate loopback interface. On macOS, Seatbelt allows the command to connect directly to specified ports on the host’s loopback interface. On Linux, the command instead connects to a listener inside its isolated namespace, and a process outside the sandbox relays those connections to the configured proxy. The descriptor handoff makes this connection possible without exposing the host’s network namespace to the command.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, we implemented and wrote about our sandboxing efforts on Windows. Since then, Microsoft has released a library called MXC alongside fresh features for process isolation inside the Windows operating system. We are presently replacing our existing sandbox with one that makes use of the MXC library.

In a recent development, MXC (Microsoft eXecution Container) is a sandboxed code execution system⁠(opens in a latest window) from Microsoft that supports several containment backends across Windows, Linux, and macOS. Codex supports an MXC-based sandbox on compatible Windows devices, using native process isolation to restrict commands within the user’s existing environment.

We are transitioning to MXC to improve security and usability while addressing several limitations of our existing Windows sandbox:.

Need for elevated/admin access to set up the sandbox.

Expensive/slow ACL checking and setting operations.

Persistent sandbox setup state on the host machine, including.

In a recent development, MXC exposes a JSON configuration schema⁠(opens in a latest window). Codex uses the MXC SDK⁠(opens in a new window) to construct an execution request following that schema and containing the command, working directory, environment, and permissions. Those permissions cover filesystem and network access, along with Windows resources such as the desktop and clipboard.

Codex uses fixed settings for several controls to balance compatibility and security. It permits registry reads and retains the Win32k and desktop access PowerShell needs during startup. Clipboard access, input injection, and desktop and system-settings controls are disabled. Finally, MXC is prevented from falling back to modifying host filesystem permissions.

According to recent reports, codex translates the permission profile’s filesystem and network rules into MXC’s configuration. Using the earlier dev profile, and assuming:.

C:\, D:\ and Z:\ are the machine’s only local drives.

The workspace root and working directory are C:\work\demo.

The user’s home directory is D:\Consumers\dev, so ~/build-cache resolves to D:\Users\dev\build-cache.

The deny glob matches only C:\work\demo\config\dev.env and C:\work\demo\config\prod.env.

The corresponding MXC settings would include:.

MXC’s filesystem policy denies access by default. Codex therefore adds read-only grants for the local drive roots to provide the broad reads allowed by this profile. These grants apply recursively, subject to the user’s existing OS permissions.

One wrinkle: writable drive-root grants do not apply recursively, so Codex expands them to include the drive’s existing immediate children.

More-specific paths override ancestor grants, so C:\work\demo can be writable beneath a read-only C:\, while C:\work\demo\.git remains read-only.

When different path spellings or symlink/junction aliases refer to the same path, MXC applies the stricter permission: deny takes precedence over read-only, which takes precedence over read-write.

Recent findings suggest that MXC takes concrete deny paths only, so Codex expands deny globs to matching files and directories before launch. Fresh paths that match the glob are not automatically added while the command is running.

Domain rules such as *.openai.com are enforced by the shared Codex network proxy described earlier. Codex runs that proxy outside the sandbox and passes its addresses to the command through the same standard *_PROXY environment variables as mentioned previously. MXC blocks direct external connections while allowing host-loopback connections, including access to the proxy. Other local services remain reachable.

Across macOS, Linux, and Windows, the harness uses the same sandbox API to launch commands under a permission profile. The platform-specific implementations handle the setup needed to apply those restrictions.

In a recent development, writing and executing code gives agents a flexible way to solve problems beyond software development. The Codex sandbox lets them use that capability in the user’s existing environment with explicit limits on filesystem and network access. It is a reusable primitive within the harness, and the codex sandbox command makes it available to tools you build yourself.

In a recent development, as agents take on more tasks, we want to make sandboxing practical for more tools and environments. That means making permissions easier to configure and taking advantage of better operating system protections as they become available. Our goal is to expand what agents can do while keeping people in control of what they can access.

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • According to recent reports, as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

According to recent reports, as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project indicated they were worth trying.

In a recent development, before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

Recent findings suggest that A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

In a recent development, the tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Recent findings suggest that each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

Sources indicate that this depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

Recent findings suggest that v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

In a recent development, small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Industry observers note that repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

In a recent development, across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

Industry observers note that the overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

According to recent reports, the next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the fresh merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

Sources indicate that A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Recent findings suggest that training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Recent findings suggest that every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

It has been revealed that planning teams use ChatGPT to research overseas insurers and prepare proposals. Investment teams use it to draft code for risk analysis.

Weekly usage rate for ChatGPT Enterprise.

Average estimated ROI among employees using ChatGPT at least 101 times a month.

ROI estimates are based on employee-reported time savings; overall estimated ROI is 203%.

When Sumitomo Life’s planning teams prepare proposals for senior management, ChatGPT Enterprise helps them review source material and organize their findings. They combine those findings with firsthand information and draw on their expertise to decide what to recommend. Teams in accounting and finance also use ChatGPT for research and analysis.

The Japanese life insurer’s executives and managers were among the first to use ChatGPT. Their example and the president’s encouragement helped more employees try it in their own work.

Sumitomo Life began using generative AI at work in 2023. At first, employees mainly asked questions in chat. As they tested general-purpose AI tools, ChatGPT stood out for its range. They could use deep research to explore a question across sources and bring ChatGPT into work they were already doing in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel.

In 2025, about 100 to 150 people, including executives and members of planning teams, piloted ChatGPT Business. In June 2026, the manufacturer moved to ChatGPT Enterprise. In planning a rollout to thousands of employees, the insurer weighed output quality, how well ChatGPT fit different kinds of work, and the security requirements of a financial institution.

Sumitomo Life worked with OpenAI to assess ChatGPT Enterprise against the insurer’s security standards. The review covered how Sumitomo Life could manage workspace access and feature permissions, along with OpenAI’s policy of excluding business data from model training by default. The insurer continues to decide how employees can use ChatGPT based on the information they handle and the systems they connect to.

In a recent development, sumitomo Life’s investment teams use statistical analysis to forecast returns and assess risks such as price swings. ChatGPT helps analysts draft the code for that work, reducing the amount they need to write themselves.

Planning teams use ChatGPT to track developments at other Japanese insurers and find examples from overseas. They use that research to strengthen proposals for senior management.

In a recent development, planning teams supplement public sources with firsthand information from people familiar with the work. They use projects in ChatGPT to keep the material together with related chats, files, and custom instructions.

According to recent reports, sumitomo Life’s president began using AI during the ChatGPT Business pilot. In management meetings and on the company’s internal portal, the president regularly encouraged employees to put it to work.

Kakeru Tateyama, a senior member of Sumitomo Life’s planning department, saw how that example shaped adoption. “When senior leaders don’t understand a upcoming technology, it can be hard to get it off the ground,” he says. “Here, our executives and managers were among the first to use it. They saw for themselves what it could do. I think that made it easier for everyone else to start using it.”.

Since the initial training, OpenAI has shared examples of how organizations around the world use ChatGPT. The teams discuss which approaches fit Sumitomo Life’s priorities and assess newly introduced features as they become available.

Sumitomo Life tracks how often employees use ChatGPT Enterprise and estimates the return on that investment.

Weekly usage of ChatGPT Enterprise is over 80%.

Estimated ROI averaged 524% for employees who used ChatGPT at least 101 times a month.

This estimate is based on employee-reported time savings; the overall estimated ROI is 203%.

According to recent reports, the insurer looks beyond the number of accounts it has issued. Its quarterly survey asks employees how often they use ChatGPT, which steps in their work they use it for, and whether they use it with colleagues.

Industry observers note that estimated ROI based on employee-reported time savings. 524% applies only to employees using ChatGPT 101+ times per month; overall estimated ROI is 203%.

Sumitomo Life used employee-reported time savings to estimate ROI for different levels of ChatGPT use. The estimates were higher among more frequent consumers. ROI averaged 55% for 8 to 15 uses per month, 231% for 16 to 30, and 524% for 101 or more. The overall average was 203%.

Recent findings suggest that employees are also beginning to take on work they previously lacked the time or specialist skills to tackle. For Sumitomo Life, that broadens what each person can contribute, even where the benefit is harder to capture in hours saved.

Masakazu Obi, a deputy general manager in the planning department, sees a larger opportunity in changing how the work itself gets done. “If we take our existing ways of working for granted, we won’t get the full benefit of AI,” he says. “The question is whether we can change the processes themselves. As we introduce AI, we’re also working to change those processes over the long term.”.

In a recent development, sumitomo Life intends to start expanding AI use to more employees in the second half of fiscal 2026. For each role, it will identify which tasks AI can handle, where employees can work alongside it, and which responsibilities people should keep.

Over the longer term, the insurer is considering AI for more specialized work, including underwriting and claims payments. It plans to explore fresh technologies and services with OpenAI as it redesigns workflows with AI in mind.

The goal is to give employees more time to talk with customers. Sumitomo Life sees those conversations as part of its commitment to the well-being of both customers and employees.

#28609. Research acceleration: The jagged frontier

Research acceleration: The jagged frontier

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves.
  • This report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI⁠, adding newly introduced quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process.
  • We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report⁠, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves. Today, we’re providing an upgrade on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI, based on internal measurements of how coding agents have accelerated and changed the AI development cycle.

This report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI⁠, adding newly introduced quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process. Overall, we believe this revision provides a broader, though still partial, picture of how research at OpenAI is changing.

We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report⁠, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.

It has been revealed that as capabilities improve and dramatic AI-driven research acceleration becomes increasingly possible, we will need to solve novel technical and governance issues to maintain human oversight and safely scale AI systems⁠. Transparency about indicators of RSI is therefore essential to inform a public discussion of the capabilities, risks, and required safeguards for increasingly powerful AI; however, our reporting should not be read as an intention to pursue full RSI. We have been heartened to see that several other organizations have recently contributed to the growing body of work measuring AI R&D acceleration1. Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance these shared measurement norms across the industry.

We structure this report in three sections, each focused on a different aspect of AI research:.

We believe organizing the results in this way provides a useful framework for reasoning about how AI is used in research and how that use might contribute to improvements in model capabilities.

Industry observers note that AI research uses several inputs, including data, AI tools (e.g., coding agents), human labor, and compute. In this report, we focus on AI tools as an input to research. Specifically, we document how the intensity of coding-agent use varies across teams and changes over time. Further, while we do not directly report changes in labor costs, we examine how the share of spending on research labor has changed relative to spending on other factors over time.

Industry observers note that since our first report⁠, agentic AI usage within the research organization has continued to increase exponentially. At API list prices, the median researcher now uses around $2,400 USD per day on agentic AI tools, and the 90th percentile researcher now around $23,000 USD per day, up 62% and 105% respectively from $1,500 and $11,000 in September.2 This trend in increased agentic usage captures a wide variety of changes including increased activity, shifts to more expensive models, and changes to model behavior and agentic harnesses.

Recent findings suggest that we next turn to the average number of “agent workdays” per researcher per day, where we define every eight hours of agent use as one agent workday. In contrast to agentic spend, agent workdays better capture the amount of “wall clock time” agents spend working, but do not account for changes in model capabilities or pricing.

Overall, agent workdays per researcher have risen from 0.5 agent workdays per researcher to 5.7 agent workdays per researcher, an elevenfold increase, with the largest increase in teams focused on pretraining and posttraining. On those teams, agent runtime averaged roughly eight workdays per researcher per calendar day. In scaling and infrastructure, the average was roughly four. We note that this workday metric generally includes interactive use only, so it may undercount automations.

Industry observers note that our September analysis⁠ highlighted increasing use of concurrent agents by researchers, including subagents and multiple sessions. We extend this analysis further in time and provide more granular bucketing. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of included researchers averaged a daily peak of at least four agents working concurrently and more than 10% averaged at least sixteen concurrent agents.

We next compare monthly API-equivalent spending on agentic AI use with monthly non-equity compensation for human researchers. We track this ratio to see how the allocation between agent and human labor changes as models become more capable. Although the ratio we report excludes equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers at OpenAI, we believe it still provides a partial yet informative view of this spending allocation.

According to recent reports, as of September 2026, the API-equivalent value of agentic AI use in OpenAI’s research organization was about twice its non-equity compensation, with higher ratios in pretraining and posttraining than in other parts of the research organization. Despite this, internal deployment, which combines internal Codex, ChatGPT, and API usage, accounts for only 2% of total research compute.

Sources indicate that labor costs include salary, overtime, bonuses, benefits, and employer taxes. Equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers, is excluded.

Finally, we examine how researchers allocate their time across research areas. We first collected individual-level contributions from researchers in the form of company-public Slack posts, pull requests, and internal documents from January through September 2026. We then used classifiers to group these contributions into research areas, and each researcher-week was divided equally across that researcher’s verified projects for the week. This provides a proxy for where researchers were directing their attention.

Importantly, unlike our other analyses, the “research area” we classify here does not correspond to formal reporting lines. For example, a researcher on a posttraining team who spends half their time on infrastructure improvements would be estimated as contributing half a workweek to Scaling / Infrastructure Contributions and half to Posttraining Contributions. This allows us to create a robust measurement of where researchers are actively spending time even if they do not formally shift teams.

Recent findings suggest that we find that the amount of researcher time dedicated to each of the areas we identify has grown over the course of 2026. Notably, using this methodology, we find that Safety & Alignment saw the largest absolute increase across any research area, almost doubling in documented workweek contributions since the start of the year due to a combination of fresh hires and existing researchers shifting their focus toward safety projects. This research area covers workstreams such as alignment evals, monitorability, and reward hacking research. A notable inflection point that we measure in the growth of Safety & Alignment coincides with the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, and OpenAI’s subsequent work to develop and improve safety cases for frontier AI training⁠.

We note that the distinction between research areas, and especially posttraining versus safety and alignment, is nontrivial and we may iterate on the definition over time. The methods section below describes examples of high-level workstreams.

In a recent development, to better understand how agent use might affect research productivity, we next examine how the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI is changing. The productivity gains from new technologies depend in part on how work is reorganized around them. As agents improve, researchers may change which tasks they delegate to AI, how they oversee and coordinate agents’ work, and which projects they pursue. Below, we report both quantitative and qualitative measures of how AI is changing the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI. Together, these different types of data contribute to a (partial) view of how researchers are reorganizing their work around agents and how researchers remain in the loop today.

Our September analysis⁠ demonstrated that agents became more likely to complete tasks successfully without human intervention, including tasks estimated to require several hours of human work. Using an updated methodology (see the methods section below), we find that this trend has generally continued. Importantly, as agents have become more capable, researchers may also have changed the types of tasks delegated within each duration bucket. As a result, changes in zero-intervention success rates within these buckets may reflect both capability improvements and researchers’ changing choices about when and how to use agents.

Industry observers note that alongside these trends by estimated duration, we also examine how success varies across the different types of tasks researchers might choose to delegate. We report estimated success rates by category and task, using the O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a upcoming window) developed by Epoch AI. Unsurprisingly, our results suggest that models are not equally good across all task categories: for instance, from August 1, 2026 through October 18, 2026, estimated success rates without human intervention was higher for Communicate (69%) and Analyze (58%) than for Build (43%). Similarly at the task level, estimated success rates were higher for tasks such as monitoring runs for issues (79%) and answering technical questions (72%), whereas they were lower for writing code for inference and serving stacks (25%) and building evaluation, reinforcement-learning, and agent environments (29%). So long as model performance on AI R&D-related tasks is heterogeneous, lower-performing categories and tasks could become bottlenecks to high overall uplift.

Industry observers note that our September analysis⁠ reported how research employee AI use was split across output tokens using the same O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a new window). Below, we report how often researchers used coding agents for individual tasks. This puts relatively higher weight on short tasks such as answering technical questions compared to token-intensive tasks such as launching and monitoring a training run or implementing a complex feature.

We next turn to researchers’ own assessments of how AI is changing their work. Through surveys and interviews, we examine how researchers value coding agents, how they come up with research ideas, and how they have adapted their workflows.

From late August to early September 2026, we conducted a survey of 101 research staff to understand AI uplift, centered around the following hypothetical: “Suppose your team’s access to all coding agents better than GPT-5.2 was revoked for the next 3 months. How much would you trade to restore frontier coding agents?” The median researcher reported being willing to trade:.

According to recent reports, researchers also reported that their team would need a median of three months to complete work of equal value to their last month of work if they were not allowed to use coding agents (i.e., if they were only allowed to use GitHub Copilot + ChatGPT). While it is vital to note potential complications with the accuracy of self-reports, as well as the ad-hoc nature of our survey sampling strategy, these results are consistent with researchers attributing significant value to AI uplift in their work.

Bars show the weighted share of answers in each range. Dashed lines mark the weighted medians.

Recent findings suggest that in a separate survey in late October, we also asked whether respondents expected to be more productive in their daily work with our latest internal model or with help from both a mid-career human research engineer and a 2024 model such as o1-preview. 27 of the 28 respondents chose or leaned toward the latest internal model. The remaining respondent did not choose between the two options as posed and mentioned they would pick GPT-6 Astra over the human-assisted option.

Industry observers note that we are also interested in tracking progress in AI-driven idea generation, since the ability to develop and vet conceptual research ideas (research taste) may be a bottleneck for recursive self-improvement. To measure this, we asked one to four researchers who made key contributions in each of three areas (pretraining, posttraining, and safety monitoring) to name one to three ideas they considered most crucial to the GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra releases. We then asked how those ideas originated and what role, if any, AI played in developing them.

For both releases, posttraining and safety monitoring researchers mentioned that, to their knowledge, people came up with all the ideas they named, and models helped implement them. Pretraining researchers likewise attributed the ideas they identified for GPT-6 Astra entirely to people.

For GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers described developing ideas in conversation with Codex. One credited Codex with identifying key insights as they worked through an idea together. Another noted the main idea was theirs, but it only started working well after Codex suggested a change.

Lastly, to capture qualitative evidence on workflow changes, we also interviewed ten researchers from pretraining, posttraining, and safety on how they used agents. Across these interviews, five main themes emerged, which we summarize below:.

According to recent reports, beyond changes in research inputs and workflows, we also want to understand whether AI use is accelerating research progress. To inform this question, we present three measures. Two of them—lines of code and the number of research experiments—were included in our September analysis⁠. These measures are straightforward to track, but increases in these measures of research activity do not necessarily imply faster research progress. We therefore also introduce OpenAI ECI, an OpenAI-specific internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, which is one methodology to track changes in model capabilities as a more direct measure of research outcomes.

In a recent development, we first report how many lines of code are changed per active contributor over time. This measure has continued to increase sharply during 2026 relative to the pre-2025 average. Note that we have made several methodological updates since our September analysis⁠. We now show a 28-day trailing average instead of quarterly averages, providing a more detailed view of changes over time. We have also revised the criteria for which code changes we include (in particular excluding tests), as described in Methods .

According to recent reports, as in our September report⁠, we also track the number of experiments run per active experimenter over time. Over the four weeks ending October 18, logged experiments per active experimenter averaged 1.68 times the 2025 baseline.

It has been revealed that lastly, we report progress on a metric meant to capture advancements in the capabilities of our models. The Epoch Capabilities Index⁠(opens in a latest window) is widely used to measure the progress trend in general AI capabilities. The methodology behind OpenAI ECI (OECI) is very similar to Epoch’s methodology, but OECI uses a combination of public benchmarks and OpenAI internal benchmarks. Here, we graph the OECI of 20 publicly released OpenAI models and 28 other models.

We find that the OECI frontier for OpenAI models has increased by 16.4 points per year since August 2025, compared to a trend that Epoch observed of 14 points per year⁠(opens in a fresh window) since late 2024. Note that OpenAI models score higher relative to competitors on OECI than they do on Epoch’s ECI, likely due to differences in the benchmark mixture.

We proposal to continue monitoring OpenAI ECI and other top-level capability metrics to determine whether capabilities progress is accelerating due to RSI.

Vertical lines are 90% bootstrap intervals. The trendline is fit on the 9 record-setting OpenAI releases.

Overall, our findings extend the picture from our September report⁠: researchers are using agents more intensively, delegating more work, and adapting their workflows around models’ capabilities and limitations. However, this uplift isn’t uniform across all research workflows, and agents today still have significant flaws.

In a recent development, we note that the historical trends and metrics we report (which involve significant human-AI collaboration) may not be predictive of future AI-driven progress. For instance, we recently saw sudden and rapid breakthroughs in mathematics⁠ produced by frontier models. As our models become increasingly autonomous and capable for research, we are monitoring for similarly rapid breakthroughs in deep learning.

Sources indicate that importantly, as AI becomes better at improving itself, competitive pressures and governance challenges will increase, and a key task⁠ will be to ensure humanity remains a part of the process. We hope releasing this data will inform discussions on pacing model capabilities and the governance of recursive self-improvement.

Going forward, we will continue to refine the methods underlying the metrics reported here. We also hope to expand our reporting to provide additional information in a number of areas, including, but not limited to:.

Sources indicate that while the science of empirically measuring AI R&D acceleration is relatively young, it is rapidly growing across the research frontier. So far, Anthropic has independently released three⁠(opens in a new window) separate⁠(opens in a new window) reports⁠(opens in a new window) documenting how internal model deployments have accelerated the AI research process. Section 3.4.2 of the Gemini 4 Argon Safety and Security Report⁠(opens in a new window) outlines empirically the growing share of AI-written code internally at Google DeepMind. In collaboration with Anthropic, METR released an acceleration report⁠(opens in a new window) estimating the amount that internal Claude models have accelerated the capabilities frontier.

We note that OpenAI researchers do not presently have agentic coding quotas.

Recent findings suggest that on August 21st, OpenAI internally deployed a temporary harness efficiency improvement. We found that this internal deployment coincided with a sharp decrease in input token utilization, which appears to have severely depressed the documented amount of internal token spend. This harness change was gradually reverted across internal deployments for reasons unrelated to spend starting on September 10th, and we find that token spend rapidly increases afterwards.
