We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

Industry observers note that in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

#28542. How fraudulent VAT refunds become clean money

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (480 w)

How fraudulent VAT refunds become clean money

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (480 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Fintech

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fraudulent VAT refunds arrive in corporate bank accounts looking like legitimate tax rebates.
  • The problem involves two connected offences.
  • Schemes range from carousel and missing trader fraud to fictitious input-credit claims and the abusive monetisation of R&D, energy and green tax credits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fraudulent VAT refunds arrive in corporate bank accounts looking like legitimate tax rebates. That is precisely what makes them dangerous, and why banks, payment service providers (PSPs) and crypto firms are increasingly in the firing line, according to a fresh analysis from RegTech firm ZIGRAM.

The problem involves two connected offences. The first is the predicate crime: submitting false or inflated VAT or tax-credit claims to a revenue authority. The second is laundering the proceeds through financial channels.

Schemes range from carousel and missing trader fraud to fictitious input-credit claims and the abusive monetisation of R&D, energy and green tax credits.

The scale is considerable. The EU VAT compliance gap reached roughly €128bn in 2023, while the European Parliament estimates carousel fraud alone costs €50bn each year. In 2024, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) was running 488 active cross-border VAT fraud investigations, with estimated damage of about €13.15bn.

According to recent reports, unlike most laundering typologies, VAT refund fraud often skips the placement stage entirely. Tax authorities pay refunds electronically, so the money starts inside the financial system.

From there, it is layered through rapid cross-border wires, circular trades between related companies, sham loans, fragmented PSP and e-money accounts, and increasingly crypto conversion. It is then integrated through property, luxury vehicles, art or reinvestment in legitimate businesses.

Recent enforcement shows how this plays out. In the EPPO’s “Fuel family” case in Italy, more than 40 missing traders generated simulated invoices exceeding €1bn, causing estimated VAT damage of €260m. Over €35m was laundered through accounts in Hungary and Romania, and authorities seized around 150 properties and a tourism resort.

The “Vortex” case, centred on second-hand luxury cars, used hundreds of shell companies across seven countries to cause losses of about €100m.

For compliance teams, the warning signs are often visible in transaction data. Key red flags include large credits from tax authorities followed by rapid scatter payments, accounts dropping back to near-zero balances after refunds, newly incorporated traders with high turnover but little substance, and round-trip trades of the same goods among related entities. Quick conversion to virtual assets and transfers to unverified wallets add further risk.

ZIGRAM recommends that investigators reconstruct account activity around refund dates, cross-check invoices and shipping documents against registries and customs records, and use network analysis to uncover shared beneficial owners and directors.

Suspicious activity reports should separate predicate suspicion from observed laundering behaviour, avoiding legal conclusions about tax liability.

Regulatory pressure is mounting. FATF treats tax crimes as predicate offences, CESOP imposes payment data reporting obligations on PSPs, and the EU’s “VAT in the Digital Age” initiative will introduce real-time e-invoicing.

As data availability grows, institutions that invest now in entity resolution, screening and adaptive transaction monitoring will be far better placed to disrupt these schemes.

It has been revealed that her mandate centres on raising the organization’s profile, strengthening relationships with customers and partners, and bringing tighter coordination to its go-to-market activity. She is also expected to reinforce Mitek’s standing as an authoritative voice in identity verification and fraud prevention, a field that continues to change quickly.

Her most recent role was heading global marketing for the API business unit of Vonage, which is owned by Ericsson. There, she worked on positioning a portfolio of multiple products, generating demand and linking marketing activity to commercial targets.

According to recent reports, before Vonage, she directed global marketing at Mitto, a Communications Platform as a Service (CPaaS) business, while it was scaling rapidly. Prior to that, she established and managed marketing teams at Telesign, which offers a digital identity and communications platform.

Across these roles, Apel has steered marketing through phases of strong growth, including helping a business increase annual recurring revenue from around $40m to $300m. Her approach puts revenue at the centre, tying brand strategy to demand generation, explaining complex technology in terms of customer benefit, lifting return on marketing spend and building closer working ties between marketing and sales teams.

Mitek specialises in helping organisations verify digital identities and prevent fraud, positioning its technology around protecting trust in online interactions.

According to recent reports, mitek CEO Edward H. West said, “Laura brings a powerful combination of strategic vision, commercial expertise and a proven ability to translate marketing into measurable business results. Her experience building high-performing global marketing organizations and accelerating commercial growth will be invaluable as we expand our impact and advance our mission of protecting trust across digital interactions.”.

Apel added, “Having spent much of my career in communications and digital identity, I’ve seen firsthand how central trust has become to every digital interaction. What excites me about Mitek is the strength of its technology, the trust it has built with customers and the opportunity to make an even greater impact as AI-driven fraud makes digital identity and fraud prevention more critical than ever.

“I look forward to building on that foundation, scaling our go-to-market engine, deepening our connections with customers and partners, and helping more organizations navigate the evolving challenges of digital trust.”.

Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 highlights strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

In a recent development, the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Recent findings suggest that proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

According to recent reports, access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been confirmed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Recent findings suggest that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports object-level audit policies, giving you fine-grained control over which database objects are audited.
  • Recent findings suggest that with object-level audit policies, you can focus on auditing the objects that matter most — for example, a single table that contains sensitive data or a specific user — without generating audit records for your entire database.
  • According to recent reports, amazon RDS provides stored procedures to create, modify, attach, detach, and drop object-level audit policies.

Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports object-level audit policies, giving you fine-grained control over which database objects are audited. You can create custom audit policies and attach them to specific tables, customers, groups, roles, and authorities in your RDS for Db2 databases.

Recent findings suggest that with object-level audit policies, you can focus on auditing the objects that matter most — for example, a single table that contains sensitive data or a specific user — without generating audit records for your entire database. Object-level audit policies complement the existing database-level audit logging in Amazon RDS for Db2. You can use both at the same time, and they operate independently.

According to recent reports, amazon RDS provides stored procedures to create, modify, attach, detach, and drop object-level audit policies. Audit records are uploaded to the same Amazon S3 bucket that you configured for Db2 audit logging.

Object-level audit policies for Amazon RDS for Db2 are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is available. To get started see the Amazon RDS User Guide.

  • AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sr. Software Engineering Manager, AlloyDB Omni.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

AlloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

AlloyDB Omni calls a local model server directly from SQL — keeping prompts, data, and responses inside your environment.

This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:.

In addition to registering your model, the above script tells AlloyDB Omni how to interpret the model’s raw output. In this example chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is part of the response inside tags. We don’t want the CoT, so our output transform function removes it.

You can use functions like ai.generate built-in to AlloyDB Omni to connect to your local model – without ever leaving the SQL client!

Try out all the AI features that AlloyDB Omni has to offer! AlloyDB Omni supports fast vector search, built-in AI functions, and more. Give them a try and build something great.

Why AI in business lending fails without full context

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (492 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Fintech

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Banks racing to embed AI across commercial lending may be overlooking a weakness that no product demo will expose: the information their models can actually see.
  • According to NCino, a single business client can involve several entities and owners, with a relationship that stretches across C&I, CRE and construction lending, and even treasury services.
  • It has been revealed that serving that client well means understanding financial performance, existing exposure, covenants, collateral and the history of past decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Banks racing to embed AI across commercial lending may be overlooking a weakness that no product demo will expose: the information their models can actually see.

According to NCino, a single business client can involve several entities and owners, with a relationship that stretches across C&I, CRE and construction lending, and even treasury services.

It has been revealed that serving that client well means understanding financial performance, existing exposure, covenants, collateral and the history of past decisions. Experienced lenders know how to piece this together. AI often does not.

It has been revealed that AI tools are already taking on intelligent document processing at intake, automating financial spreading, answering credit policy questions in natural language and monitoring covenants. The time saved on rekeying data and chasing documents can be redirected towards building relationships.

In a recent development, however, AI works only from the data within its reach. If that is limited to one application, one document set or one system, the model makes its judgement in a silo. A banker in the same position would recognise the gap and look for what is missing. An AI model frequently will not, and its output may still appear complete. The result can be worse than if a person had done the work.

This is why evaluating AI by its capabilities alone is risky. Point solutions can look impressive in a demonstration, but a tool that sees only part of the relationship can only do part of the job. The real question is what lending context sits behind those features. That includes borrower and financial data, exposure, credit policy, documents and decision history.

That context has to live somewhere. A system of record offers a reliable, current view of the borrower, the relationship, credit history and decisions taken. It may be centred in a single lending platform or assembled from connections across multiple systems.

Recent findings suggest that gartner’s Market Guide for Commercial Loan Origination Solutions maps commercial credit across its full lifecycle, from client acquisition and intake through underwriting, approval, booking, servicing and loan management. Along the way it interacts with core banking, CRM, and risk and compliance systems.

Keeping that record complete is a moving target, and Gartner’s recommendations provide a useful framework. First, connectivity: institutions should assess prebuilt integrations, ecosystem breadth and whether APIs follow industry standards. Second, adaptability: a componentised, modular architecture allows banks to add products and adjust workflows without overhauling the entire platform.

Industry observers note that third, explainability: as AI-supported credit decisioning grows, Gartner stresses model governance, transparency, data security and guardrails. Institutions remain accountable for how AI-supported decisions are used.

The stakes are rising. Gartner notes that many CLOS vendors now offer similar AI features, making functionality alone a weak differentiator. Banks that secure the right context first will be best placed to turn AI into strategy rather than just another tool in the stack.

Acorda, a London-based anti-fraud startup set up by three former Monzo employees, has secured £1.8m in a pre-seed round as it builds a network that lets banks and payment providers pool scam intelligence.

According to DealRoom, Eileen Burbidge has backed the round. The startup will put the capital towards bringing banks and payment firms onto its data-sharing network.

The platform gives financial institutions a secure way to exchange scam risk indicators linked to the person or business receiving a payment, in the moments before the funds leave the sender’s account.

With this information, the sending bank can judge how risky the recipient is before releasing the transfer. Acorda’s aim is to reduce the number of scams that succeed while also lowering the volume of legitimate payments wrongly flagged as fraudulent.

The raise arrives as UK payment companies come under increasing pressure to tackle authorised push payment (APP) scams, in which victims are tricked into sending money themselves. Firms also now carry financial responsibility for compensating those who lose money to these schemes, raising the cost of failing to intervene.

Acorda operates a fraud data-sharing network designed for banks and payment providers, focused on preventing scams at the point of payment rather than identifying losses once money has already moved.

Industry observers note that the firm was founded by Robert Parrish, Jhamat Mahbubani and Sam Kelsey, who between them spent over three years developing fraud prevention systems at Monzo. At the digital bank, Parrish headed product for the authorised fraud team, Mahbubani ran machine learning and Kelsey oversaw engineering.

In a recent development, acorda’s founders are betting that shared data, not isolated defences, will decide who wins the fight against APP fraud. For executives who need to see these shifts before the market does, FinTech Global delivers the strategic intelligence that shapes decisions across the sector.

AI raises the stakes as insurers struggle to evidence skills

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Zing365 has found that nearly every senior insurance leader believes their firm satisfies its CPD and regulatory training obligations, yet 41% say proving that learning has taken place is their biggest compliance challenge.
  • The study arrives as insurers respond to the FCA’s policy statement PS25/21.
  • The hours requirement continues to apply to long-term insurance staff, and professional bodies may impose their own rules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Zing365 has found that nearly every senior insurance leader believes their firm satisfies its CPD and regulatory training obligations, yet 41% say proving that learning has taken place is their biggest compliance challenge.

The study arrives as insurers respond to the FCA’s policy statement PS25/21. From 9 December 2025, this scrapped the mandatory 15-hour annual CPD threshold for insurance staff who are not CII qualified and do not work in investment roles. The responsibility for maintaining suitable knowledge and competence still sits with firms, but logged hours can no longer serve as proof of it.

The hours requirement continues to apply to long-term insurance staff, and professional bodies may impose their own rules.

The data comes from The UK Insurance Skills & Competency Index 2026, which underpins Zing365’s white paper, From compliance to competence – How insurance builds measures: and maintains capability in the age of AI.

Censuswide carried out the independent survey of 151 senior managers and insurance brokers with responsibility for training, competence or corporate strategy.

Industry observers note that confidence levels were striking. Some 99% of respondents believe their organisation reliably meets mandatory CPD and regulatory learning requirements, while 84% describe their learning and development programmes as very or extremely effective.

It has been revealed that the 41% figure combines four separate answers on the single greatest compliance-learning challenge: measuring effectiveness (14%), tracking progress or completion (11%), recording and reporting CPD (9%) and demonstrating competence (7%). The report notes these are practical difficulties and do not show that firms are unable to prove compliance.

It has been revealed that respondents rated coaching and mentoring (51%) and on-the-job learning (48%) as the most impactful training methods. Zing365 believes firms should record how this kind of learning is put into practice, alongside formal course records, to gain a more complete view of capability.

Artificial intelligence features heavily in the findings. A total of 82% say AI is reshaping their business or is being actively deployed, and 40% rank AI and digital skills among the hardest capabilities to build. Almost a third (32%) expect AI skills to demand the largest workforce investment over the next two years, close to triple the next category, cyber security awareness, at 11%.

According to recent reports, zing365 argues that training should test whether staff can spot gaps, challenge unsupported conclusions and justify decisions reached with AI support. The survey did not examine how often employees defer to AI. The FCA regulates AI through existing frameworks such as the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, which places weight on accountability and oversight as new tools are adopted.

Industry observers note that zing365 managing director James Read stated, “Confidence is not the same as evidence. Many firms will have strong learning programmes, but the question is whether they can show what their people are able to do, where they need support and what changed as a result of their training.

“Greater flexibility over CPD makes decisions about what training to deliver, and how to assess it, more important. Counting hours was never enough to establish competence. Firms need a clear basis for judging whether learning is helping people carry out their responsibilities.”.

Sources indicate that read added, “An AI-generated summary can look convincing and still omit an important policy condition that changes the decision. If someone accepts it without checking, completing an AI course tells us very little about whether they were prepared for that responsibility.

“For compliance and training leaders, the key question is what happens when an employee encounters an answer that looks right but is wrong. Can they recognise the problem, explain their reasoning and know when to seek help? That is the capability learning needs to build and assessment needs to test.”.

#28531. Latest Update: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3325 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post indicates you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Recent findings suggest that reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

In a recent development, if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

According to recent reports, beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Sources indicate that attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

According to recent reports, the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

According to recent reports, the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

In a recent development, beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

According to recent reports, every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Strategy for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

According to recent reports, the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

According to recent reports, pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel proposal. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

In a recent development, launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

According to recent reports, beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

Recent findings suggest that for faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Industry observers note that both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

Sources indicate that we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

It has been revealed that † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

In a recent development, don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

Industry observers note that the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

Industry observers note that the setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

Recent findings suggest that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Industry observers note that training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the fresh weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

It has been revealed that the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

It has been revealed that sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Sources indicate that upgrade: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

In a recent development, evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

Sources indicate that the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

It has been revealed that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Recent findings suggest that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

Industry observers note that for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

Industry observers note that first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

Recent findings suggest that for a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

In a recent development, beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

In a recent development, that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

Recent findings suggest that this is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts.
  • Recent findings suggest that openAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches.
  • According to recent reports, we’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts.

Recent findings suggest that openAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test⁠(opens in a new window), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.

According to recent reports, we’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.

Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.

According to recent reports, shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.

How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF.

OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:.

Sources indicate that live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

It has been revealed that trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

In a recent development, hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

According to recent reports, the Shirudo technical walkthrough⁠(opens in a latest window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host⁠(opens in a new window). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here⁠(opens in a new window).

In a recent development, shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.

Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.

Sources indicate that we will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.

Industry observers note that openAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo⁠(opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart⁠(opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.

Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab⁠(opens in a new window).

Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar⁠(opens in a fresh window).

According to recent reports, we’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, upcoming shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub⁠(opens in a new window), read the docs⁠(opens in a new window), and let us know what you find⁠(opens in a new window).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SBS, a provider of regulatory reporting software for financial institutions, has teamed up with professional services firm Deloitte to build a reporting solution that gives European banks a clearer line of sight from raw data to submitted figures.

The collaboration is built on BIRD, the Banks’ Integrated Reporting Dictionary, and is designed to help lenders keep pace with shifting obligations such as IReF and SRB VDS. It also addresses the growing emphasis on data traceability and control set out under BCBS 239/PERDARR.

At the centre of the partnership is a planned BIRD-native product running on SBS’s existing technology.

The tool is intended to show banks exactly how their underlying data is transformed into reported numbers, strengthening their oversight of data, workflows and regulatory submissions. Greater visibility should make reports simpler to justify and to audit.

Rather than requiring a wholesale overhaul, the solution can be rolled out step by step, allowing institutions to extend their current reporting set-up as regulatory demands intensify.

Each firm contributes distinct strengths. SBS supplies an established regulatory reporting platform alongside long experience working with financial institutions. Deloitte adds deep knowledge of BIRD and regulatory reporting, covering both reporting processes and operating models.

Recent findings suggest that reflecting BIRD’s principle of being developed “for and by banks”, the two companies proposal to agree a joint roadmap with banks themselves. As the project advances, participating banks will decide priorities and influence how reporting rules are built into the product.

Deloitte partner regulatory reporting Peter Schaap stated, “Consolidation in the regulatory reporting market makes meaningful choice more important for banks, particularly with significant changes such as IReF and SRB VDS on the horizon. Banks should have a say in how new reporting requirements are translated into practice and the flexibility to adopt changes in a way that fits their existing processes. SBS’s regulatory reporting software and experience with financial institutions make it a strong collaborator in bringing that choice to banks.”.

Industry observers note that SBS CCOO Raouf Mhenni added, “Financial institutions across Europe trust SBS as a long-term partner, and that trust shapes how we work. Together with Deloitte, we want to give our clients a real say in the solutions they rely on, and a clearer view of the data and processes behind them. It is about delivering outcomes they can count on.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ​​Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Db2 now supports renaming databases in place.
  • According to recent reports, ​​Database rename simplifies workflows such as replacing a database with a restored copy.
  • In a recent development, ​​Database rename is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is offered.

It has been revealed that ​​Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Db2 now supports renaming databases in place. You can rename a database on your DB instance by calling the new rdsadmin.rename_database stored procedure. Previously, renaming a database required you to back it up and restore it under a new name. With rename, the database keeps its data in place, so it's faster than backing up and restoring the database.​.

According to recent reports, ​​Database rename simplifies workflows such as replacing a database with a restored copy. For example, after you restore a copy of a database from a backup, you can rename the original database, and then give its name to the restored copy, without changing your application connection strings. Database rename runs as a background task that you can monitor with rdsadmin.get_task_status.​.

In a recent development, ​​Database rename is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is offered. To get started, see the Amazon RDS User Guide.​​.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, torchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • In a recent development, torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • It has been revealed that starting Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, torchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

In a recent development, torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

It has been revealed that starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Industry observers note that text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Industry observers note that here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

In a recent development, nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

In a recent development, the command below debuts training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Industry observers note that training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Recent findings suggest that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, owners can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

#28525. Breaking: Can AI investment give RegTech firms a lasting competitive edge?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1999 w)
