Breaking: Can AI investment give RegTech firms a lasting competitive edge?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fintech

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, regTech firms are investing heavily in AI, but the scale of that investment alone will not determine who comes out ahead.
  • Recent findings suggest that regTech Analyst and Parker & Lawrence Research recently published a major industry report examining the global state of RegTech in 2026.
  • FinTech Global recently sat down with several leading players in RegTech to get their thoughts on these findings in a second part of a two-part series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, regTech firms are investing heavily in AI, but the scale of that investment alone will not determine who comes out ahead. As AI capabilities become increasingly accessible, the competitive advantage will lie in how effectively firms translate them into better products, stronger customer outcomes and more differentiated offerings.

Recent findings suggest that regTech Analyst and Parker & Lawrence Research recently published a major industry report examining the global state of RegTech in 2026. As part of their findings, they looked at the return on investment on the commercial benefits of AI, and how this differed based on business size.

FinTech Global recently sat down with several leading players in RegTech to get their thoughts on these findings in a second part of a two-part series.

Why are some firms in the market generating significantly higher returns from AI than others?

In the view of Sarah French, CRO of TaxTec, the difference often comes down to whether organisations are investing in technology to solve a clearly defined business problem or simply investing in AI because they feel they should.

She remarked, “There is a significant difference between introducing automation and fundamentally improving how an operation functions.”.

Sources indicate that “For example, in financial services, many processes remain dependent on manual investigation, fragmented information, specialist knowledge and multiple operational touchpoints. Automating individual tasks may deliver incremental efficiencies, but the greater value comes from looking at the entire operating model and identifying where complexity can be removed.”.

For French, organisations that understand their operational challenges, establish clear objectives and measure outcomes are better positioned to realise meaningful returns from their technology investments.

Meanwhile, Areg Nzsdejan, CEO of Cardamon, remarked that the interesting thing for him in the survey was how little separates the groups of reduced manual effort.

According to recent reports, he remarked, “50.6% of the highest-ROI group report it, compared with 47.5% of the lowest. The gaps are much wider for faster onboarding, approvals or reviews, at 43.4% versus 27.5%, and faster product launches or market expansion, at 18.1% versus 2.5%.”.

These, he makes clear, are reported benefits, so the figures do not establish what caused the higher returns.

For the Cardamon CEO, however, they do suggest a useful question: has the time saved changed what the business can do?

“Automating a task creates limited commercial value if the same approval queue still holds everything up,” he stresses.

In the view of Anthony Quinn, CEO of Arctic Intelligence, the organisations who are seeing real returns from AI aren’t the ones automating the most tasks.

“They’re the ones who’ve tied AI to a specific customer outcome, such as faster, more defensible risk decisions, and built it into the product rather than bolting it on,” he explained.

In the view of Andrew Davies, global head of FCC strategy at ComplyAdvantage, the gap usually comes down to how the investment was scoped, rather than which model was selected.

He explained, “In our 2026 State of Financial Crime Report, 48% of compliance leaders reported that their firms have dedicated projects and budgets for AI in financial crime. Almost as many (46%) reported that their AI budget is confined to specific teams or siloed parts of the technology stack. Ultimately, an investment scoped to a single function returns value to only that function.”.

In a recent development, for Davies, there is a second, less comfortable explanation. Almost nine in ten respondents – 88% – admitted that including AI in a proposed compliance modernization program increases the likelihood of gaining approval and securing resources.

He remarked, “AI is simply easier to fund than most compliance technology, which means some programs are approved on the strength of the “AI” label rather than the viability of the business case. Firms that defined their desired outcomes first – such as fewer false positives, faster remediation, or better risk scoring – have something to measure returns against. Firms that funded the technology first simply do not.”.

How can RegTech firms move beyond automation to drive growth and commercial value?

In the opinion of Davies, buyers are already making that shift. He highlighted how when asked about the outcomes they have seen or expect from agentic and predictive AI, respondents named increased efficiency first at 54%, followed by improved customer experience and satisfaction at 51% – significantly ahead of cost reduction at 26%.

He commented, “The commercial case for AI in compliance is being built on driving growth rather than just savings: faster onboarding, fewer legitimate customers held in review, and less friction between a firm and its revenue.”.

For the FCC head, the real opportunity lies in the work that companies have not yet automated.

It has been revealed that davies stated, “Auto-remediation of level-one alerts is presently the least-implemented capability at 32%, behind suspicious activity detection at 55% and transaction monitoring at 53%. And while 95% of compliance leaders agree automation of routine work would be highly helpful, not a single respondent reported already having that capability – an unmet need in the highest-volume, lowest-judgment part of the workflow.”.

Meanwhile, for Nzsdejan, he suggested firms should start with a business decision that compliance work is delaying.

Sources indicate that “For a new product or market, a firm needs to establish which obligations apply, what it already covers and what has to change. At Cardamon, we speed up that assessment by mapping regulatory obligations against existing policies and controls, helping teams identify gaps and the work needed to close them earlier,” he said.

With this, firms can reduce compliance delays to a product launch or entry into a fresh market, while keeping the same standard of review.

In a recent development, he added, “RegTech providers should measure the whole process. Time to an approved decision, rework and cost per completed assessment are more useful than the number of documents summarised.

“For the provider, reusable workflows can also reduce implementation costs and make it economical to serve more customers. That advantage depends on how much specialist work is still needed for each deployment.”.

Quinn, however, is succinct, “Automation cuts cost, but it’s a race to the bottom. Commercial value comes from using AI to deliver insight customers couldn’t get before.”.

For French, the opportunity extends well beyond reducing processing time or operational costs.

“Technology can enable financial institutions to deliver services that would previously have been commercially difficult to provide, improve the experience for their clients and scale operations without a corresponding increase in resources,” she stated.

Industry observers note that french stated that withholding tax recovery is a good example. “Historically, the operational effort involved in identifying, documenting, submitting and tracking reclaims has created barriers to delivering these services efficiently. Technology can help change that equation by centralising information, improving workflow management, reducing manual intervention and providing greater transparency over recovery opportunities.”.

It has been revealed that the commercial value, she added, is not simply in doing the same work faster. It is enabling institutions to identify additional opportunities, improve service delivery and make previously resource-intensive activities commercially viable.

She went on, “AI may accelerate this further, but its value needs to be measured against tangible business outcomes rather than the sophistication of the technology itself.”.

What separates firms that successfully scale AI from those struggling to realise its potential?

The firms that struggle to scale tend to treat AI as a project, said Quinn. The ones that succeed, he believes, treat it as an operating model, with clean data, clear governance and a roadmap tied to revenue.

On the other hand, French made clear her view that successful organisations recognise that technology adoption is as much an operational and strategic challenge as it is a technical one.

She said, “Scalability requires reliable data, clear processes, effective governance and integration with the wider technology environment.”.

According to recent reports, in addition, it also requires an understanding of where human expertise remains vital. For example, inhighly specialised areas such as tax and regulatory operations, technology should support experienced professionals by removing repetitive activities and improving access to information, rather than assuming every decision can or should be automated.

She commented, “The organisations that succeed will be those that combine technological capability with genuine subject-matter expertise and a clear understanding of their clients’ operating environments.

Industry observers note that “Ultimately, competitive advantage will not come from simply having AI. It will come from how effectively that technology translates into better outcomes for clients, stronger operational resilience and sustainable commercial growth.”.

Nszdejan believes that the scalers make it possible to repeat a good result.

In a recent development, he explained, “A pilot can work because a few experts quietly correct the output. Scaling requires those corrections to become test cases, clear review rules and improvements to the underlying workflow.

Recent findings suggest that “Teams need realistic examples of both routine and difficult work, and they need to test again when the model or source material changes. Someone must own the process and decide when an uncertain answer goes to a person.”.

The economics for the Cardamon CEO should involve ongoing maintenance. If each upcoming customer requires another layer of manual checking, the cost of delivery will keep rising with revenue, he said.

In a recent development, in the view of Davies, the bar has moved, and the regulator is helping set it. Speaking at the Bloomberg UK Policy Series on October 19, 2026, Jessica Rusu, the Financial Conduct Authority’s Chief Data, Information and Intelligence Officer, outlined the FCA’s vision for an “agentic regulator”.

Sources indicate that the watchdog is developing its own agentic tools to automate supervision, with initial deployments monitoring around 9,000 smaller wholesale firms filing transaction reports. It is also preparing to oversee the anti-money laundering controls of a further 60,000 firms expected to enter its remit from 2028.

Recent findings suggest that according to Davies, the significance extends beyond the scale of these operations. As regulators themselves adopt AI to strengthen supervision, firms face growing pressure to demonstrate that they can monitor, explain and assure how their own systems behave in production.

Recent findings suggest that AI governance can no longer be treated as a periodic exercise. It must become a continuous function, embedded throughout the deployment lifecycle. This is increasingly the dividing line between firms scaling AI successfully and those struggling to move beyond pilots.

According to recent reports, however, for Davies, the biggest obstacle is often not the technology itself, but the architecture supporting it. Organisations operate an average of seven separate systems for each compliance activity, spanning customer screening, transaction monitoring, case management and regulatory reporting.

Deploying AI across this fragmented infrastructure risks reproducing the very data gaps, inconsistencies and operational blind spots that firms are trying to eliminate.

According to recent reports, adoption figures illustrate the gap between ambition and execution. For standard AI in customer screening, 93% of firms are using, piloting or evaluating a vendor solution, with 62% having successfully moved into production. Agentic AI presents a different picture. Although 73% are using, piloting or evaluating the technology, just 33% have reached production.

Davies believes that successful AI deployment depends on more than selecting the right model. Firms must first establish the data foundations, system connectivity and governance needed to support it. Increasingly, these are not simply prerequisites for scaling AI. They are also essential to keeping pace with a regulator that is becoming more technologically capable itself.

It has been revealed that davies concluded, “The firms seeing real returns from AI didn’t start with the model. They started by defining what a good outcome looks like, then ensuring they could measure it continuously.

“This is no longer just good practice – when the regulator is running its own agentic tools, a system that cannot demonstrate how it behaves in production becomes a liability rather than an advantage. Almost every firm expects AI to deliver. Far fewer have built the data foundation that allows it to do so.”.

It has been revealed that amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime instances now support Amazon EC2 G7 instances, powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. Runtime instances run your agents on Amazon EC2 instances while AgentCore handles provisioning, patching, scaling, and lifecycle management. G7 instances give agents that do 3D rendering or model inference another GPU option, alongside families such as G6e and G7e.

In a recent development, to use G7, add G7 instance types, from g7.2xlarge to g7.48xlarge, to the allowed instance types of your capacity provider. AgentCore installs the NVIDIA drivers on the instance, so standard container images run GPU workloads without bundling drivers. For example, an agent can render 3D scenes or run a vision model on its own GPU, in sessions of up to 14 days.

In a recent development, G7 instances on runtime instances are available in select AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), and Asia Pacific (Sydney). You are charged for managing the provisioned compute, in addition to your Amazon EC2 costs.

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1385 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and upcoming Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

It has been revealed that you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

Sources indicate that FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

Industry observers note that you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

It has been revealed that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each upcoming token goes through the model as a single row, so the major matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

In a recent development, MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Sources indicate that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Recent findings suggest that the decoding kernel indicates up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

According to recent reports, working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Sources indicate that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

It has been revealed that audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

According to recent reports, token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Sources indicate that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

According to recent reports, you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Recent findings suggest that work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

According to recent reports, once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Sources indicate that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

It has been revealed that bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Industry observers note that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A major thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.
